The imperial envoy Jiang Tinggui arrived and respectfully proclaimed the Sacred Edict:
"As we are currently afflicted by excessive drought, an order has been issued to pray for rain.
A period of seven days is set as the limit for its attainment."
Bu Kong replied: "The one whose words must be followed like those of a silken thread is the sovereign;
the one who must follow the issuing of the imperial decree is the minister."
I humbly submit that Your Majesty extends your vision to all four quarters and reaches your hearing to all four directions;
as high heaven listens to the lowly, you harbor a heart of deep anxiety for the people’s labor.
This may be called the ultimate clarity of the sovereign.
Having received the imperial decree,
he immediately established a solemn place of practice.
Without exception, they have united their strength and harmonized their hearts,
so that Your Majesty’s natural perfection may rely upon the bequeathed teachings of the Buddhas;
our humble sincerity is most profound.
Sincerity moves the divine;
there was no need for the signs of the *yanwu* dance,
as the grace of Heaven has already descended upon all under the sky.
Below, it accords with the hopes of the people;
above, it fulfills the Sage’s heart.
With feet treading the ground and hands dancing, I am overcome with joy and cannot contain my exultation.
I respectfully submit this memorial to announce my congratulations.
I, the Śramaṇa Amoghavajra, speak with sincere joy and delight.

On the first day of the sixth month in the seventh year of the Dali era, the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa of Daixingshan Temple, the Special Advancement (Tetjin) and Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, the Greatly Vast Wisdom (Da Guangzhi) Amoghavajra, presents this memorial to the Emperor, the One of Precious Response, the Primordial Sage, the Martial and Civilly Wise. The Emperor’s Rescript: The Venerable One’s wondrous conduct is perfect and luminous; his great compassion provides vast salvation.
With profound concern for state and family, his benevolence permeated all living beings.
He purified the ritual altars and offered earnest prayers for sweet rain;
day and night he diligently invoked the true sages to manifest their presence.
Within less than ten days, a gentle rain was brought forth;
as the sprouts thus flourish constantly, a bountiful harvest is now within reach.
Reflecting upon my own meager virtue, I am filled with a sense of shame and renewed diligence.

A Petition for the Selection of Virtuous Monks for the Memorial Pagoda of the Former Master and the Stone Ordination Platform Courtyard of the Eastern Capital; One Poem on the Memorial Pagoda Courtyard of the Tripitaka Master of Great Propagation at Jianfu Temple in the Eastern Capital.
Please draw the names of seven eminent monks from among the various monasteries.
Regarding the aforementioned pagoda complex,
our late master Amoghavajra was specially granted it by His Majesty the Xuanzong Emperor during his lifetime.
As the years and months passed long,
the temple buildings crumbled and collapsed,
and offerings at the incense burners were neglected.
As there is no one to sweep and sprinkle [the grounds],
we now request that seven virtuous monks (mahāsthavira) from various monasteries be appointed to preside over that temple,
performing repentance and recitation during the six periods of the day and night to cultivate the three mysteries of yoga for the sake of the nation.
To continue the traditional legacy of the master-disciple lineage,
the Ancient Stone Precept Platform Hall (Kuksedan) of the Sarvāstivāda school at this temple requested seven eminent Vinaya masters from among the various monasteries.
Every year, a precept platform (sīma) is established for the monks.
This aforementioned Precept Platform Hall was founded during the lifetime of the Venerable Amoghavajra by the donation of his robes and alms bowl.
On the day Amoghavajra received full ordination,
he also made a sincere vow to permit the joint restoration of the temple.
I, Bukong, have unworthily received the imperial grace;
I hope that the jade mirror may be opened once more,
so that I may behold the ancient regulations of the Great Master.
I look forward to the turning of the Golden Wheel once again.
I now request that you establish the plaque for the Sarvāstivāda Precept Platform Hall and select seven virtuous monks by lot.
Throughout the four seasons, he expounded and chanted the Vinaya for the monastic community;
during the six periods of the day, he performed the practice of the Three Mysteries (Sammitsu) on behalf of the state.

This was submitted as a memorial by the former *Teijin* (Special Advancement), Acting *Hongluqing* (Court of State Ceremonial), Tripitaka Śramaṇa of Daixingshan Monastery, the Great Widely Wise Amoghavajra.
Regarding the aforementioned matters concerning the selection of monks and the establishment of official quotas for this monastery,
please ensure that vacancies are continuously filled.
As for the labor levies imposed by the prefectures and counties, as well as all other monastic affairs:
Furthermore, we request that the various temples be exempted from differing regulations. The details are respectfully set forth as listed above.

The Secretariat and Chancellery issue this notification to the Great and Widely Wise Amoghavajra. Notification: By Imperial Decree, it is ordered that this be complied with. This notification is issued in accordance with the decree. Thus notified on the sixteenth day of the sixth month of the seventh year of the Dali era. Notification from Yuan Cai, Minister of the Secretariat and Chief Counselor; Wang Jin, Minister of the Chancellery and Chief Counselor; Li Shi, Minister of War and Chief Counselor; and the Grand Master of Ceremonies concurrently serving as Director of the Secretariat. We request that Dharma Master Chaowu be assigned to Huadu Monastery to perform the ritual for the Six Bodhisattvas, and that one copy of the "Ritual for the Lecture on the Six Bodhisattvas" be prepared. Furthermore, we request six statues of the Great Bodhisattvas for Huadu Monastery. Right: A memorial submitted by the Special Advancement, Acting Courtier of the Court of State Ceremonial, Tripitaka Śramaṇa of the Great Xingshan Monastery, the Great and Widely Wise Amoghavajra.
Having previously received the Imperial decree to construct the aforementioned merit-making work,
we now invite Dharma Master Chaowu to preach the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra before the image for the sake of the State.
I hope that Your Majesty will honorably cultivate [this practice] so as to cleanse the ears and eyes of all living beings; thus,
my humble sincerity shall find fulfillment.
The 4th day of the 8th month, the 7th year of the Dali era. The Clerk Shang Xiú issues this notice to the Chief Administrator Liu Yìjí and Zhū Chángrú.

Imperial Decree for the Establishment of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Monasteries Throughout the Realm. One decree for the establishment of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva monasteries throughout the realm, issued by the Secretariat-Chancellery (Zhōngshū Ménxià). Notice addressed to the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra.
It is hereby decreed by imperial edict that within the monasteries for monks and nuns in the capital and throughout the empire,
a superior location shall be selected in each to establish a court for the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, each local prefecture and commandery official was commissioned to immediately oversee the repairs.
Once the decoration and painting of the Mañjuśrī images were completed,
each official was required to draw a depiction of their appearance and submit it for imperial review.
No further separate construction shall be permitted outside the monasteries. This notification is issued in accordance with the Imperial Decree.

Notification dated the sixteenth day of the tenth month in the seventh year of the Dali era. Notification from Yuan Zai, Minister of the Household and Chief Councilor; Wang Jin, Minister of the Palace Gate and Chief Councilor; Li [Name], Minister of War and Chief Councilor; and Xie [Name], Grand Master of the Court of State Ceremonial and Director of the Secretariat, in response to the Imperial Decree establishing Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Cloisters throughout the realm. A single memorial expressing gratitude for the decree establishing Mañjuśrī Cloisters in all temples, together with the reply to the śramaṇa Amoghavajra.
I have humbly observed the special imperial edict of the sixteenth day of this month,
which directs that within each monastery for monks and nuns throughout the capital and the empire,
a superior location shall be selected to establish a shrine for the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Amoghavajra heard that those who paint and decorate images of Mañjuśrī with colored pigments must perform the ritual methods of the Sage alone.
His virtue moved Heaven;
his bounty moistened all living beings.
He was like the sun and moon suspended in the sky.
I, Bukong, am truly joyful and deeply grateful; I leap with delight.
I humbly submit that Your Majesty has opened the profound creation of the Dharma King and cleared the path for this extraordinary field of merit.
The construction of a true image of Mañjuśrī,
so that all under heaven may gaze upon it in reverence,
brings especially profound and auspicious fortune to the assembly of monastics.
Furthermore, the Holy One Mañjuśrī is the teacher of all Buddhas and patriarchs;
through his great compassion and vast vows, he does not take formal enlightenment,
so that his guidance of the Mahāyāna for the benefit and happiness of beings shall be without end.
Formerly, Śākyamuni Tathāgata gave a prophetic prediction:
"The teachings of the One Vehicle shall flourish in the Middle Kingdom;
there shall surely arise a most sagacious sovereign who will govern the state according to the principles of the Mahāyāna."
For over eight hundred years,
there have been many emperors, kings, sages, and worthies throughout history;
yet truly, none has been like Your Majesty.
How fortunate I, Amoghavajra, am to have been born to encounter this sagely dynasty and to cultivate the Mahāyāna.
I serve Mañjuśrī and constantly recite these sacred mantras specifically for the sake of the state.
Every time I have been graced by your protective mindfulness,
your kindness and virtue have grown ever deeper;
day and night I reflect upon this, yet find no way to repay it.
I did not expect that, suddenly, Your Heavenly Compassion would be so universally pervasive.
Shedding tears for my long-held sincerity,
I have neglected both sleep and food, unable to bear the mixture of grief and joy.
I am overwhelmed by the utmost sense of honor and responsibility.
I respectfully submit this memorial of congratulation, conveyed through the imperial envoy Yang Guizhen, for Your Majesty’s perusal.
I, the śramaṇa Amoghavajra, express my sincere joy and delight. Respectfully stated.

On the twenty-seventh day of the tenth month in the seventh year of the Dali era, the *Tetjin* (Special Advance) and Acting *Hongluqing* (Court of State Ceremonial), Tripitaka Śramaṇa of Da Xingshan Monastery, Da Guangzhi Bukong, presented this memorial to His Majesty, the Emperor Yuan Sheng Wenwu of Baoying. The Emperor’s decree read: “The Great Sage Mañjuśrī has long since attained Perfect Enlightenment.”
He rescued living beings from the three realms and subdued the venomous dragon atop the five peaks;
his path of compassion was profound.
His merit in providing vast salvation is so profound that he has caused the community of Śākyas to likewise take refuge [in him].
He is a master of the Tripiṭaka and a preeminent teacher from the land of India.
This is truly a cause for profound consolation and satisfaction.
I acknowledge your congratulations.

I request that one temple be established in each of the two streets of the capital to lecture on the Imperial Decree regarding the newly translated *Mahā-ākāśagarbha-sūtra*. Yuan Ying, a Great Virtue of Zhangjing Temple, requests that Baoshou Temple provide the lectures; Dao Ye, a Great Virtue of Zisheng Temple, requests that Ximing Temple provide the lectures.
The above memorial was submitted by the Right Special Advancement, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Tripitaka Śramaṇa of Daixingshan Monastery, the Greatly Vast Wisdom Amoghavajra:
"The aforementioned scripture has been promulgated in accordance with the Imperial Edict."
It has never before been expounded.
If it were not praised, how could the holy achievements be manifested?
The aforementioned virtuous masters have all completed their commentaries.
I request that the temples on both the East and West Streets each regularly lecture on this sutra,
so that the river of merit may flow secretly and silently,
providing supreme support for the Emperor’s longevity.

The Secretariat and the Chancellery issue this notification to the Great Master of Vast Wisdom, Amoghavajra. We hereby notify you that, in accordance with the Imperial Decree, it is "fitting to proceed accordingly. This notification is issued in compliance with the Decree. Therefore, this notification is issued on the eighth day of the first month of the eighth year of the Dali era. Issued by Yuan Zai, Minister of the Secretariat and Chief Councilor; Wang Jin, Minister of the Chancellery and Chief Councilor; Li Shi, Minister of War and Chief Councilor; and the Grand Tutor concurrently serving as Director of the Secretariat. On the fifteenth day of the second month, an Imperial Decree was issued to commence work at the Translation Hall of Daxingshan Temple.
The Great Sage Mañjuśrī’s State-Pacifying Pavilion was constructed.
The monk Xiuyan of great virtue served as the supervisor, and the śramaṇa Huisheng served as the assistant supervisor.
The śramaṇa Amoghavajra stated:
Having humbly received the imperial decree to translate this sutra,
I was sustained by divine power; thus,
the work of producing these volumes has been completed.
The names of the monastics and laypeople who received the oral transcription of the realized meaning, along with the date, year, and location, are all listed at the end of this volume.
Last month, on the fifth day of the fifth lunar month, the submission was completed;
by the grace of Your Majesty’s benevolence, permission has been granted for its public proclamation.
Amoghavajra is truly joyful and truly apprehensive; he is both deeply humbled and profoundly grateful.
Amoghavajra has heard that the one who established the teaching is the Tathāgata.
As for the propagation [of the Dharma]: who other than a sagely sovereign could carry out the Buddha’s work?
We humbly entreat Your Majesty to turn the moon and sun upon the Yellow Path.
He lets fall the rain and dew upon all living beings,
moistening their very natures;
the monastic community especially rejoices as they receive his abundant grace and care for themselves.
It is not yet known what its retribution will be;
however, this sutra is the source of all practices.
The sublime designation of the Pure Land is fully endowed with the adornments of the Bodhisattvas’ great vows and merits, as well as samādhi, supernormal powers, and the Dharma-seal of the Tathāgata.
Even the merit of briefly hearing of it and rejoicing therein is inexhaustible.
How much more so, then, are the merits of reading, reciting, receiving, and upholding this teaching beyond measure?
I hope that through these benefits of the Dharma, I may repay even a small fraction of my gratitude;
I particularly beseech Your Imperial Majesty’s compassionate favor.
It was decreed that seven monks from the great monasteries and three monks from the small monasteries throughout the empire shall,
at the time of the inauguration of the newly established Mañjuśrī Temple, lecture upon and recite [the scriptures] for the sake of the state;
should any vacancies arise, they shall be filled in succession.
I strive to ensure that the Dharma-sound and the lamp of transmission remain unextinguished,
so that all lands may enjoy eternal peace and the sacred personage may be forever protected.
In the utmost sincerity of my earnest entreaty,
I respectfully submit this memorial for Your Majesty’s perusal. I,
the śramaṇa Amoghavajra, most humbly pray and with profound trepidation, respectfully state:

On the day of the sixth month in the eighth year of the Dali era, the *Tejin* (Special Advance) and Acting *Hongluqing* (Director of the Court of State Ceremonial), the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Da Guangzhi Bukong, submitted a memorial concerning the decree to demote the Abbot of Xingshan Temple, Yuánjìng, to the Sīyuǎn Temple in Hénán. Decree on the Demotion of the Abbot of Xingshan Temple, Yuánjìng, to Return to the Sīyuǎn Temple in Hénán: One Copy. The Abbot of the Great Xingshan Temple, Yuánjìng, was originally assigned to Lùhùn in Hénán Prefecture.
A Memorial from the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa of Daxingshan Monastery, the Right Special Advancer and Acting Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, Bukong, Greatly Vast Wisdom, concerning Xiansi Yuansi:
The aforementioned monk has recently been relieved of his duties as an inspector of monastic affairs.
Fukū was subsequently appointed as the head of Xingshan Temple.
As reported by his disciples, such as Qian and others,
that monk personally took charge of the monastic administration.
They encroach upon and damage the permanent property of the Sangha,
and they ruin and demolish monastic dwellings to construct private rooms for themselves.
He unreasonably exploited his family members;
he engaged in manual labor with his concubines and gathered groups of nuns to stay overnight without guarding against suspicion.
Consequently, he was investigated by the Capital Prefecture of Jingzhao.
As these deeds have become manifest,
I fear that you will be subjected to legal punishment according to the Dharma;
within the gates of the Dharma, this is truly a cause for shame.
I humbly entreat you to preserve his religious robes and not deprive him of his monastic title,
compelling him to return to his original temple in Lu-hun and granting him the opportunity to reform.

For the sake of the state, this was performed as a ritual observance. Upon receipt of this memorandum, it is issued in accordance with the Decree. Issued on the thirteenth day of the seventh month in the eighth year of the Dali era. Memorandum from Yuan Zai, Vice Director of the Secretariat and Concurrent Chancellor; Wang Jin, Vice Director of the Chancellery and Chancellor; Li [Surname], Minister of War and Chancellor; and the Grand Master of the Court (Situ), concurrently Grand Secretary (Zhongshuling): A Memorial for the Submission of the *Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetra-guṇavyūha-sūtra*. One copy of the Memorial for the Submission of the *Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetra-guṇavyūha-sūtra*, consisting of one fascicle of the *Mahāryamañjuśrībuddhakṣetraguṇavyūhasūtra* in three volumes, together with a jeweled casket. [Right side: Previously, Amoghavajra received an Imperial Edict ordering him to translate this scripture.
By the grace of Heaven,
all matters have been successfully accomplished;
the Chinese and Sanskrit texts have been compared and collated.
The refined determination of the phonetics,
the dates, the locations, the names of the scribes, the witnesses, and the monastics and laypeople— all these are inscribed within the volume.
Furthermore, the deeds, origins, and causal conditions concerning Mañjuśrī are recorded therein.
This sutra fully records everything from the initial generation of the bodhicitta until the attainment of perfect enlightenment and the adornment of the pure land—
the fundamental principle of all Buddhas.
The gateways of the Bodhisattva’s practice clearly manifest the reality-mark of the non-arising of sentient beings within the dharma-realm;
its merit is vast and great.
This scripture is rare among others.
I pray that through this supreme cause, it may further assist the imperial destiny.
I humbly entreat that it be proclaimed throughout the realm to bring blessings to all living beings.
I particularly pray for Your Majesty’s divine grace.
Regarding the seven monks at the newly established Great Monastery of Mañjuśrī and the three monks at the Small Monastery:
they shall remain within the Mañjuśrī Monastery for a long time to lecture upon, proclaim, recite, and practice [the scriptures] for the sake of the state.
Where there were deficiencies, they were filled;
thus the lamp of the Dharma was kept alight without interruption.
Among the spirits and all classes of beings, who would not have rejoiced?
Fortuitously, on this day of the Wheel-Turning King’s birth and this auspicious assembly of devas and humans,
we pray that these great blessings may further increase the Mountain of Longevity,
and that the stream of the Dharma may augment the Sage’s ocean.

The aforementioned monk,
whose observance of the precepts was pure and refined, was esteemed by the assembly;
he previously served as the Abbot-General, managing the affairs of the monastery.
From beginning to end, he has remained as one;
his diligent efforts have been quite manifest.
Now, this temple lacks a presiding abbot.

Relying upon his administrative supervision, we humbly pray that he be fully appointed as the Abbot (*vihārasvāmin*). The Secretariat and Chancellery issue this notification to the Great Master of Vast Wisdom, Amoghavajra.

This notification is issued in accordance with an Imperial Edict stating: "It shall be so. Upon receipt of this notification, it is to be executed according to the Edict. Thus notified on the fourth day of the eighth month of the eighth year of the Dali era. Notification by Yuan Zai, Minister of the Secretariat and Chief Counselor; Wang Jin, Minister of the Chancellery and Chief Counselor; Li Shi, Minister of War and Chief Counselor; and the Grand Master of the Court of State Ceremonial and Chancellor, who was granted the title of Lord of the Jade Flower (*Jinghua zhenren*) and bestowed with one entire collection of the *Tripitaka*. **Table of Thanks for the Bestowal of One Entire Collection of the Tripitaka as Lord of the Jade Flower** A single table of thanks for the bestowal of one entire collection of the *Tripitaka* as Lord of the Jade Flower, together with the response from the Śramaṇa Amoghavajra.
The Inner Chamber Attendant-in-Chief, Wu Xiuyue, respectfully proclaimed the Imperial Decree:

"The *Zhengrui zhenren zhēnrú jīngāng yīqiè jīng* (The True Scripture of the Vajra of the Reality of the Perfected Person of the Essence of Jade), one entire canon consisting of five thousand and fifty scrolls."
All were made with sandalwood-fragrant rollers and bound in multicolored silk covers;
the entire collection of scriptures was composed of various fragrances.
Sandalwood desks support incense burners of gold and precious gems,
where clouds and mists shine upon one another.
The sun and moon alternate in their course;
their radiant light and fragrant splendor overflow the streets,
bestowing non-emptiness upon all.
He was accommodated at our monastery,
where he was assigned to recite scriptures, offer worship, and receive [the sacred image].
His joy and gratitude were intertwined.
I do not yet know by what merit I may respond to Your Majesty’s profound grace; yet,
upon careful reflection, I find that according to the sacred scriptures of the Buddhas, even one who merely upholds them shall obtain boundless merit.
I hope that through these supreme causes, I may repay even a ten-thousandth part of my debt of gratitude.
I have respectfully dispatched fourteen persons to perform long-term recitations.
May the True Persons and True Suchness be as firm as adamant, and may the precious reign of the Sage Emperor flourish anew for ten thousand kalpas.
Unable to contain my heart’s boundless joy,
I have respectfully entrusted this memorial to the imperial envoy Wu Xiuyue to submit my expression of gratitude for Your Majesty’s knowledge.
The Śramaṇa Amoghavajra, with sincere joy and trepidation, respectfully addresses these words.

On the eighteenth day of the tenth month of the eighth year of the Dali era, the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Da Guangzhi Amoghavajra, holding the rank of Special Advancement and Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, presents this memorial to the Emperor, the One of Precious Response, the Primordial Sage, Martial and Civilly Virtuous. The Emperor’s decree: “The Tripiṭaka Master’s pure conduct is profound and subtle; may the Holy and True One grant his protection.”
The merit of walking in meditation and reciting the scriptures is boundless;
I respectfully enshrine this Tripitaka in a fragrant stupa,
praying for auspicious blessings.
May You protect and bless Qionghua,
so that all ailments may be forever eliminated and auspicious goodness may flourish ever more.
How could such extraordinary favor be described as merely a matter of thanking You for Your grace?

A Memorial of Thanks for the Imperial Bestowal of Red Coins, Fried Cakes, and Other Items for the Lifting of the Main Beam of the Mañjuśrī Pavilion. A Memorial of Thanks for the Imperial Bestowal of Fried Cakes, Cash, and Other Items for the Lifting of the Main Beam of the Mañjuśrī Pavilion. One scroll. Submitted by the Śramaṇa Amoghavajra.
Regarding the Manjusri Pavilion, it was previously honored by an imperial decree to commence the laying of the ridgepole on the fourteenth day of this month; thus,
the Emperor’s grace has been bestowed upon us in its full measure.
A special vegetarian feast for a thousand monks was bestowed;
two hundred strings of red coins for the laying of the beams,
and two thousand fried cakes.
Two thousand pieces of *húbǐng* (Hu-bread),
two hundred strings of tea,
and ten jars of fragrant decoctions.
Ten *he* of honeyed rice cakes on a tray,
fifteen sweet oranges,
and forty stalks of sugarcane.
Imperial messengers followed one after another upon the roads;
food and drink overflowed the streets;
and the assembly was fully satiated with the precious delicacies of the imperial table.
The celestial kitchen’s broth and tea have universally reached both officials and commoners;
Your Majesty’s grace is excessive,
and what means do we have to repay it?
The wise all say:
since the Buddha-dharma first came to the East nearly a millennium ago,
have the kings of antiquity not cultivated merit?
In terms of vast and expansive beneficence, there has truly never been one like His Majesty the Emperor today.
How fortunate Amoghavajra is to have been born to encounter such a sagely dynasty and further receive the transmission of the mantras!
To praise this sublime transformation,
even if one were to offer a hundred bodies and recite with diligent devotion day and night,
how could one possibly repay even a ten-thousandth part?
I am overcome with the utmost joy and trepidation.
I respectfully entrust this memorial of thanks to the Imperial Commissioner Li Xiancheng for presentation to Your Majesty.
I, the śramaṇa Amoghavajra, truly feel both gratitude and shame. I respectfully submit this.

On the tenth day of the twelfth month of the eighth year of the Dali era, the *te jin* (Special Advance) and acting *Honglu Qing* (Director of the Court of State Ceremonial), the Tripitaka Śramaṇa of Daxingshan Monastery, Da Guangzhi Bukong, presented this memorial to the Emperor, the One of Precious Response, the Primordial Sage, the Martial and Civilly Wise. The Emperor’s reply stated: "The transmission of the teachings has been harmonized with the Buddhist palace."
His resonant voice flowed throughout the Eastern lands;
he propagated the sacred scriptures and upheld the true Dharma.
May his merit sustain all living beings,
and may blessings gather within his household and realm;
he has established this pavilion for Mañjuśrī.
At the outset, you sent beams from the Xiangcha Temple and provided offerings to assist in the vegetarian feast;
there is no need for a formal letter of thanks.
A Memorial on the Prayer for Rain by the Tripiṭaka Upādhyāya, and a Memorial of Thanks for the Rain, along with the Response from the Śramaṇa Amoghavajra.
Recently, at the end of last winter, the snow ceased.
Now that the first month of spring has come to an end,
the lingering heat still persists;
the people in every household suffer from parching heat, and the Emperor’s heart is filled with deep anxiety and compassion.
Taking the blame upon himself for others,
he prayed to Heaven with focused contemplation;
truly, he obtained a timely response.
The spring moisture spreads universally;
rivers and plains are drenched in abundance;
grasses and trees flourish with blossoms.
Thus we know that the sagely virtue moves Heaven,
and divine response follows like an echo;
when a single person has a resonance with it, [the response follows].
All things have been illuminated and revived;
we are overcome with the utmost joy.
We respectfully take this opportunity to present this memorial of congratulation through the Imperial Messenger Li Xiancheng for Your Majesty’s information.
The śramaṇa Amoghavajra, with sincere joy and gratitude, respectfully addresses these words.

On the fifth day of the second month in the ninth year of the Dali era, the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Da Guangzhi Amoghavajra, holding the special rank of *Tetjin* and serving as Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, presents this memorial to the Emperor, the One of Precious Response, the Primordial Sage, Martial and Civilly Virtuous. The Emperor’s decree: "Since winter, there has been little snow."
With deep concern for the agricultural outskirts,
he issued separate mandates to his various officials to offer prayers throughout the mountains and rivers.
The ancestral altars receive blessings and protection,
and the spirits and deities harbor their favor;
the clouds hasten forth in early spring.
As the rain drenched the middle fields,
the Upādhyāya, mindful of his family and country,
reverently invited [the deities] to the place of practice.
The time for abundance and harmony is approaching;
therein lies consolation and joy.
You may know that I offer my congratulations.

A Memorial of Condolence for the Passing of the True Man (Zhuren) Qionghua; one memorial of condolence for the passing of the True Man Qionghua, together with a response to the words of the Śramaṇa Amoghavajra.
I humbly receive the news that the Realized One Qionghua has passed away.
Your Imperial Compassion is deeply stirred above,
and your sorrow extends to all who pass by.
Wu-k'ung was naturally simple and humble; he lay prostrate upon his pillow for a long time.
Yet, by the grace of the Sage, he did not regard me as an ordinary monk, but sent me to raise this true person as his daughter.
The intensity of this pain is indeed double that of ordinary circumstances.
When a True Person fails to maintain their composure,
the physical vessel of the true cause cannot help but falter.
Unable to overcome my illness to enter the inner quarters for empowerment,
I intended to support myself with a staff yesterday on the twenty-seventh to request an audience; however,
upon reaching the southeast corner of the inner city wall, I received the tragic news of the True Man’s passing.
Turning back on the way,
I was moved with longing for my past life;
there is no means by which I may take my final leave.
My grief cannot be fully expressed;
my pain is indeed profound.
I humbly beseech Your Sacred Majesty’s compassion to permit me to proceed with all my strength to the funeral of the True Man on the second day of the coming month.
That my thoughts have been turned toward the fulfillment of my sincere intentions is truly both a source of sorrow and joy; thus,
I constantly make offerings with utmost devotion and resolve my vows.
I direct my thoughts upward toward all the Buddhas,
hoping to rely upon their spiritual power to protect the deceased soul.
I humbly pray that Your Majesty’s sacred mind will deign to grant its clear discernment.
Once Bukong has somewhat recovered from his illness, I hope to support him and offer my consolation.
I respectfully submit this memorial for Your Majesty’s information.
Sincerely sorrowful and deeply grieved, the śramaṇa Amoghavajra respectfully addresses these words.

On the twenty-ninth day of the fourth month in the ninth year of the Dali era, the śramaṇa of the Tripitaka, Da Guangzhi Amoghavajra, holding the rank of Special Advancement and Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, presents this memorial to the Emperor, the One of Precious Response, the Primordial Sage, Martial and Civilly Wise. The Imperial Rescript: "O True Man, throughout your life you were one for whom I held deep affection."
Because she had been long afflicted by illness, she relied upon me as a field of merit;
out of compassion, my preceptor raised her as his own daughter.
Yet, her condition was so grave that no remedy could save her.
My grief and compassion are truly profound.
It has been a long time since the Upādhyāya fell ill;
his physical constitution has become frail and weak.
Furthermore, you should take care of yourself;
do not exhaust yourself to the point of ruin.
I shall hear of your full recovery soon.

Memorial of Gratitude for the Bestowal of White Silk on the Fifth Day of the Fifth Month; One Memorial of Gratitude for the Bestowal of White Silk, together with a Reply to the Śramaṇa Amoghavajra. Having humbly received the imperial inquiry proclaimed by the Palace Messenger Yuan Yingquan: [The Emperor] bestowed white silk as a gift. [I] submit this one memorial of gratitude for the bestowal of white silk, along with a reply to the śramaṇa Amoghavajra.
I have reverently received the sacred questions proclaimed by the Palace Messenger Yuan Yingquan.
I was further granted white silk and other gifts;
receiving them with profound shame and trepidation, I am at a loss as to what I should do.
I humbly submit that:
In my care for life, I lacked a proper method and thus became entangled in the suffering of illness;
despite my efforts, I failed to overcome it, and my precious flower was cut down by a premature calamity.
Yet, I have once again been bathed in Your gracious favor.
Your repeated inquiries have reached me;
I am overwhelmed by a sense of profound sorrow and gratitude.
I respectfully submit this memorial to express my thanks and bring it to your attention.
The Śramaṇa Amoghavajra, with utmost reverence and trepidation, respectfully addresses these words.

On the fifth day of the fifth month in the ninth year of the Dali era, the Śramaṇa, Special Advancement (Tejin), Acting Minister of State for the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu Qing), Daguangzhi Amoghavajra, submits this memorial to the Emperor, the One of Precious Response, the Primordial Sage, Martial and Civilly Wise. [Imperial Edict: The Venerable Master’s spiritual practice is perfectly enlightened.
His compassion pervades all universally.
Having suffered from chronic illness since youth,
his anxious concern is exceptionally profound.
Touched by the seasonal offerings, I labor to express my gratitude.
This is the single letter left behind by the Tripiṭaka Upādhyāya; I hereby announce it universally to the fourfold assembly of disciples.
The Great Teachings are collectively vast and profound, deep and expansive;
who can fathom the source of the Yoga Secret Mantras?
Since my childhood, I have left the household life.
Relying on his teacher to study the academic curriculum,
he searched through the Sanskrit manuscripts for over twenty years,
applying himself with diligent effort day and night.
I have humbly submitted myself to receive your instruction and am now about to be granted the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* in its four thousand stanzas;
yet alas, my accumulated transgressions are so profound and heavy.
My late teacher has passed away;
having no one to rely upon for shelter,
by what means shall I advance in my practice?
For this reason, he traveled far to India,
braving the perils of sea voyages,
and studied yoga extensively.
He paid homage to the sacred sites and received the authorization (*anujñā*) for the Dharma treasury consisting of one hundred thousand verses.
He then returned to his imperial homeland, bringing these teachings with him.
He traveled through auspicious lands to propagate his teachings.
Thus, in a single day, he was honored as the Imperial Preceptor for three successive emperors,
and the sovereigns bestowed upon him the esoteric transmissions and ritual seals of Yoga Tantra.
From this point forward, as the present Sage extensively propagates the teaching,
the eighteen assemblies of the most profound Yoga are all fully established;
each of the thirty-seven classes of holy beings shall practice them one by one.
Whenever entering the dōjō,
one should recite the mantras according to the prescribed times;
even the Emperor of Nine Palaces and Ten Thousand Chariots should constantly contemplate the mind of the five wisdoms.
In the imperial court, the hundred officials all hold the seals of the three mysteries.
I have personally presided over consecrations for more than thirty years,
and there are many disciples who have entered the mandala to receive the Dharma.
The five lineages were refined and established as eight branches;
these subsequently fell into decline one after another until only six persons remained.
As for those who attained it:
Jin’ge Hanguang, Silla Hui-chao, Qinglong Hui-guo, Chongfu Hui-lang, Baoshou Yuan-jiao, and Jue-chao.
If future students have doubts,
you all must provide them with instruction so that the lamp of the Dharma shall not be extinguished.
Thus you shall repay my kindness;
all the more so, as I have reached the age of seventy and my physical strength is gradually declining.
Among you, there are many who are still young; therefore,
I first entrust my affairs to the monks and disciples of this temple, such as Huisheng and others,
who have attended to me since their youth.
He has been reverent and diligent without negligence;
having labored for many years,
he is truly worthy of compassion.
Although you have not yet received the five sections [of the teachings],
if you can thoroughly master and practice even a single deity until you attain Buddhahood, that will suffice.
Each of you must exert yourselves as if I were still alive.
You must dwell together in harmony;
if you cause harm to the community,
I shall not protect you.
"I have received and maintained the vajra, bell, and ritual mace, along with a silver plate, a rosary of bodhi seeds, a crystal rosary, and a pair of joined bowls.
I present these all together as an offering to the Holy One; please enter within."
As well as Baoshou, Huadu, and the disciples of Xingshan and other monasteries:
while I am still alive,
you all rely upon me.
I shall protect and mind you.
After my passing into parinirvāṇa,
you all shall rely upon this kingdom.
One must be loyal toward the nation.
Strive with diligence and sincerity to maintain mindfulness for the sake of the country;
thus the land will be secure and the people at peace.
My vow is fulfilled.
To Tanjing of the Qinglong Temple,
I have previously bestowed the Great Dharma mantras.
As for the ritual seals (mudrās), you have not yet obtained them;
please transmit them to me on my behalf.
Furthermore, regarding the lay disciple Gongde, who served as Li Kaifufu: [insert appropriate instruction].
Having received the Dharma from me for over thirty years,
he has been diligent and sincere,
his filial piety profound and deep.
When Heshang Nanshai came and went on his journey to inquire about the Way,
Jingying Honglu personally attended to his needs and provided offerings.
He first bestowed upon him the five sections of the *Yogācāra* treatises.
Seventeen: The five physical forms further increase the secret [teachings].
My silver ritual implements—the five-pronged, three-pronged, and single-pronged vajras, as well as the bell—are all left to you, O Kaifu (Governor).
Recite them with mindfulness and uphold them; you shall swiftly realize *siddhi*.
The master monks within the monastery shall come and go and conduct inspections as they did during my lifetime;
you must ensure that all affairs are maintained in peace and that those above and below live in harmony.
Since Supervisor Li Dafu first began overseeing me, he has not deviated from his purpose in the slightest.
His petitions and reports on our travels have all accorded with the Imperial Will;
he has not merely assisted the State.
It is also for the sake of Bodhisattvas who protect the Dharma;
Samantabhadra’s Secret [Teaching] should be received and upheld,
so that by following in the footsteps of the Mahāyāna, one shall surely attain realization.
I leave these four silver *vajra-karmas* and the wheel for you to receive and uphold;
by reciting them, you shall realize Bodhi.
Protect the Buddha-dharma as if I were still present in the world.
The worthy Zhao Qian and I occasionally took up the pen for the purpose of translating the scriptures;
others who transcribed the texts also contributed their efforts.
"If you love leaving the household life, I shall provide you with the opportunity to hear and perform music;
if you prefer remaining in secular life, you may remain at peace there as well.
Later, I obtained one fascicle of the Mañjuśrī Sūtra.
One fascicle of the *Ratnakūṭa-bhāṣya-mantra-vidhi* and one fascicle of the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* have been translated,
though they have not yet been presented for imperial inspection.
I have recorded these matters for my submission to the capital.
My devotion to the Precious Vajra grows deeper by the day;
he is cautious, filial, and obedient.
As for the recitation of mantras, he became even more diligent;
he remained within the monastery to dwell and make offerings together with the practitioners and novices of the monastery.
From the virtuous and noble above down to your slaves below,
you shall serve as an official to petition for their ordination.
As for Sudhana and Yaśas, they are both granted freedom as commoners and permitted to go wherever they please.
It is also acceptable for him to remain in the monastery according to his own wishes.

However, as his elder brother Tingxiu is currently in the South Sea and wishes to have him attend to him, the Prefect has also requested that you release him so he may care for his parents; thus, Qiao shall be made a member of this household.
For a long time, he has followed me into the inner quarters.
The Sage also recognized him;
he was always employed in specialized tasks and exerted himself more than anyone else.
Regarding the petition for the renunciation of the world by Official Li:
there are two oxen on his estate,
valued at approximately ten or more strings of cash.
I shall provide funds from the permanent endowment to serve as the purchase price,
redeeming [the property] so that it may fulfill all necessary functions within the monastery.
All the banners, flowers, statues, and various meritorious objects within the maṇḍala— such as woolen rugs, carpets, copper vessels, porcelain, and conch-shell cups—
are all to be relinquished and placed within the maṇḍala below the Mañjuśrī Pavilion.
It shall be used for offerings forever;
it must not be diverted, diminished, taken outside, or lent to others.
As for my own person, my clothing, and all else, I have already relinquished them entirely. I possess eighty-seven taels of gold and two hundred twenty-five taels of silver.
He further dedicated these as offerings to the two temples of Jinge and Yuhua on Mount Wutai for the purpose of renovation and merit-making:
all household furniture, utensils, wooden implements, ironware, earthenware, beds, mats, felt rugs, stools, hoes, and all other miscellaneous items whatsoever.
I have bestowed both [of these] for the use of this monastery.
When disciples come and go, they must have a place to lodge.

These scriptural cases shall be placed within the storehouse on the upper floor of the hall; as for that storehouse and the scriptures, they are hereby granted by imperial decree to be installed and maintained within the monastery.
"You shall constantly recite, maintain, and burn incense as offerings to protect it for the sake of the state;
it must not suffer any fragmentation or loss.
I shall petition the Sage to have a pavilion constructed."
Place the image of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva below and install the scriptures in both Chinese and Sanskrit above;
let this serve as a field of merit for the nation, to be venerated in offerings for all generations.
The main pavilion has been largely renovated,
yet the carpenters remain indebted for the unfinished decorations; the porticos,
corridors, gatehouses, and monks' quarters have likewise not yet been completed.
"Regarding all the fragmented, scattered, and remaining timber from the rafters,
you and the Great Officer shall consult together to properly report [the matter] to the throne so that the restoration may be completed.
Once the pavilion is finished, you shall establish a community of twenty-one monks on behalf of the State."
By reciting the sutras and performing invocations,
may the Holy One’s life-span be eternally sustained,
and may my original vow be fulfilled.
The pagoda site for the Venerable Master at Tōkyō, along with the temple buildings, monastic quarters, and estates—
these you shall also manage and establish for me. Furthermore, there are the wagons and oxen,
the estate south of the Hiao River in Hu County, the land recently purchased, the rice fields obtained adjacent to the Goshoku-gawa River, and the vegetable garden south of the street.
I have donated both [these items] to the monastery, to be kept beneath the Mañjuśrī Pavilion in the ritual hall.
They shall be used for the perpetual support of the preceptors and monks, as well as for offerings such as oil, incense, charcoal, and firewood.
In no case may they be removed from the monastery or used for personal consumption.
No outsiders shall be permitted to obstruct or encroach upon this estate.
Its auspicious fields and purple-groves shall increase twofold the permanent endowment.
The formal deeds for these estates are hereby entrusted to the monastery.
I address my disciples once more:
You must understand that human life is impermanent; who can escape this?
The relationship between teacher and disciple is based on intimacy through the Dharma and its meaning, which differs from that of flesh and blood;
it is entirely distinct from worldly relations.
If you follow my words, you are my sons and disciples.
If you disobey my command, it shall not be in accordance with the Dharma.
After my life has ended,
none of you shall wear mourning garments, nor shall there be weeping or longing remembrance.
Remember me by diligently engaging in recitation;
this is how you repay my kindness.
Furthermore, do not wastefully squander wealth or employ elaborate rites and deportment for the funeral.
Furthermore, do not leave the burial site empty and waste human effort;
simply take a single bed and devote yourself entirely to recitation and chanting.
They escorted him to the outskirts and performed the cremation according to the ritual.
They collected the ashes and empowered them through mantra.
He then immediately dispersed the assembly.
Furthermore, one must not set up an altar for his spirit or paint my likeness.
Even among the seventy-two disciples of the Confucian scholars, there were those who performed mourning through the heart (xin-sang).
In the transmission of my teaching of empowerment, it is by no means like this.
You, my sons, are born from the Buddha’s own mouth and transformed by the Dharma; having obtained a portion of the Buddha-Dharma, you are identical to the body of Samantabhadra.
Practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra and abiding in the mind of Samantabhadra,
one becomes perfectly luminous, vast, and all-pervading.
The five wisdoms manifest simultaneously;
practicing in this manner accords with my heart.
Why trouble yourselves with such weary and restless pursuit of matters that are contrary to the Dharma and bring no benefit?
This is what I declare to you;
you must all comply with this my instruction.
Fearing that there may be no basis for verification in the future,
I further request that the names of the three dignitaries, the year-steward,
and the assembly of disciples be recorded as a witness. Thus informs the Upādhyāya.

The Official in Charge, Guangyuan; the Clerk, Xi Sheng. The [blank] day of the sixth month, the ninth year of the Dali era. Below is the Petition Submitted by the Tripiṭaka Master on His Deathbed. One petition: A Statement Submitted by the Tripiṭaka Master on His Deathbed. The Śramaṇa Amoghavajra says: [Text follows...]
Abhāva (Bukong) has served his former master for more than twenty years;
he early on received the imperial favor.
For over thirty years, I have practiced the Dharma-gates of Yoga.
Having been favored by the grace of successive sagely emperors,
my special favor has deepened ever since Your Majesty ascended the throne.
He was granted the Yellow Gate for his private residence and descended from the Purple Microcosm to inquire after the Way; thus,
accumulated favors were layered upon one another.
The sun and moon follow one another in succession;
though my devotion be sincere and earnest,
how could it repay even a ten-thousandth part?
Yet, like dew or lightning, life is difficult to sustain;
like the *púliù* tree, one easily succumbs to decay.
From the moment I first lay prostrate upon my pillow...
From spring until summer, Your Majesty has shown profound compassion,
inquiring after [the patient] repeatedly;
imperial messengers and renowned physicians have appeared one after another along the roads.
Yet, as with a disease at the vital point (gāohuáng), life is difficult to sustain despite acupuncture and medicine;
how could this nature of arising and ceasing be preserved through attachment or regret?
Since last night, it has suddenly [begun to fail].
Suddenly his strength and vigor utterly withered, and he felt his body was no longer his own;
in a fleeting instant it vanished,
and his spirit and mind grew increasingly faint.
I offer my apologies for having disobeyed the Sacred Court;
I cannot bear the longing [for my homeland].
Now that my years have exceeded the midpoint of a full lifespan, they are not in vain.
It was not that his life ended prematurely;
rather, it was because in the past he had crossed the South Sea and traveled throughout the Five Indies.
He sought out what he had not yet heard and practiced what he had not yet understood;

the Great Master accepted his imperial mandate and ascended Mount Qingliang;
having received the Emperor’s grace, he returned to the capital city.
As for all such verified responses,
it is difficult to recount them in full; through them,
one finally realizes that the nature of flowers in the sky is devoid of arising or ceasing.
How could the functioning of True Suchness (tathatā) have coming or going?
Throughout his service, he translated a total of eighty-three scriptures comprising one hundred and twenty fascicles, all by imperial decree.
He has already issued the catalog for inclusion in the Tripitaka,
and furthermore submitted a memorial requesting that all monasteries throughout the empire take Mañjuśrī as their presiding Elder (upādhyāya),
while establishing cloisters and erecting his images therein.
He was appointed as the Protector (Baoli) of the State Border,
where he renewed his profound reverence.
In the eighth year of the Dali era, an imperial decree was issued.
At the Xingshan Main Monastery, he further constructed a Golden Pavilion for Mañjuśrī.
Prohibited wealth was drawn from within [the treasury],
and the sons of artisans arrived.
The precious parasol hung from the ninefold heavens;
the imperial incense was likewise bestowed by the Sovereign alone.
A multitude as vast as motes of dust emerged as if surging forth from the earth.
It was as if the music of the Celestial Emperor were being performed in the void.
On the eleventh day of the sixth month in the ninth year,
an edict was issued granting the Grand Master the rank of Kai-fu Yi-tong San-si.
He was enfeoffed as Duke of Sugu with an appanage of three thousand households;
all other matters remained as before.
Your inquiries were most thorough and comprehensive,
and your favor was abundant and manifold;
you condescended to the dignity of the Northern Pole to observe the rites due to a venerable teacher.
The gifts of banners and images,
the bestowals of jade and silk— imperial edicts fill the baskets,
and imperial envoys appear one after another.
From ancient times until now, there has never been one whose pure faith was like that of our Emperor,
nor whose sincere devotion was like that of our Master.
Since the age of twenty until his fifties, when he followed his heart's desire, the Great Master has spent over fifty years [in this service].
Every day at the four periods of the day, he performed recitations at the ritual hall;
from ascending to the imperial throne to descending to his ordinary couch.
In the span of a single kṣaṇa, there has never been any interruption.
That the dark-green pines on ten thousand ridges maintain their color despite enduring bitter frost serves as a testament to their upright integrity.
How much more so when entering a crimson gate is like entering a thatched cottage;
for five years, three times he wore robes as tattered as those of a quail.
Though he might gallop upon a qilin, [he remains unchanged].
It constantly abides in the purity of the nine dhyānas;
standing alone, it is beyond comparison.
It is like the great, all-pervading mani jewel, which originally possesses no fixed color.
"His brilliance has ceased with him; what does he have to do with me?
He was truly a master of the mysteries of mantra."
This is the great treasure of the Dharma King. Alas!
A Bodhisattva should perceive the un-abiding mind as accomplished;
thus does the Tathāgata, like a firm forest, deliver the multitudes of sentient beings.
Manifesting a slight illness,
he knew the time of his departure.
On the fifteenth day of that month, he commanded his disciples to present a memorial to offer his formal resignation.
He entrusted his final affairs to others,
shaved his head, bathed,
and lay down on his right side with one foot upon the other.
He passed away while staying there at the age of seventy and with fifty years of Dharma-ordination.
At that time, torrential rain poured down;
suddenly, the heavens opened up.
The Emperor’s grief was profound within the nine layers of the palace.
The court was suspended for three days.

He was posthumously granted three hundred rolls of silk, two hundred bolts of cloth, three hundred thousand coins, four hundred *shí* of rice and flour combined, as well as fragrant oil, firewood, charcoal, and various provisions for seven additional memorial services.
Furthermore, two million two hundred and twenty-five thousand coins were bestowed to construct a spirit-stupa,
which the entire realm may behold with reverence.

Furthermore, by imperial decree, Li Xiancheng, a high-ranking attendant, was appointed to oversee the affairs, and Li Yuancang, a Grand Master of Ceremonies with the rank of Kai-fu-yi-tong-san-si, was appointed as the Protector of Merit.
On the sixth day of the seventh month, he was accorded a state funeral at Shaoling Yuan to the south of Feng.
On that day, the Secretariat and Chancellery issued an imperial decree posthumously conferring upon him the title of Minister of Works (Sikong) and the posthumous name "Great Discerning,
Correct, and Vast Wisdom Amoghavajra," the Tripiṭaka Master and Upādhyāya.
Furthermore, they dispatched the Inner Attendant Liu Xianhe.
The imperial edict was proclaimed and the sacrifice performed;
fragrant wood was brought forth from within the palace and burned upon the sacred coffin.
The rites of cremation were performed.
That the temple pond dried up and its flowers withered was a sign that his end had come;
that in a dream the banner tilted and the pavilion collapsed was a period of ominous warning.
How could these signs of the twin śāla trees turning white and the sensation of the waters of the cave-flowing upstream have occurred in former times?
Among the ministers and the hundred officials, there were none who had received the Dharma-seal who did not mourn with deep sorrow.

His disciples—the four groups of followers, numbering some ten thousand, including the Śramaṇa Dazhi, Director of the Palace Attendants and Inspector of Daxingshan Monastery, as appointed by imperial decree to oversee the constant cultivation of merit—were all present.
I lament that the great night has returned to its darkness and grieve that the lamp of wisdom has been extinguished forever.
Though my talent is meager, I have recorded his illustrious legacy;
I followed him as he flew with his staff, mistakenly joining the assembly of Kumārajīva.
Having the honor of attending the assembly of the Qin Emperor,
I imagine the weeping of Gao Chai;
all are alike in their vision of blood amidst luxuriant flowers.
Thus, to extol the teaching that is beyond words,
I shall praise the Dragon among Dragons with these verses, which say:
The explanation of characters is the mantra itself; Heaven gave birth to my teacher as he turned the palm leaves.
Having realized the fundamental source within the gates of the Dragon Palace, the elephant-vehicle proceeds afar and the celestial music flourishes.
My task being accomplished, I shall enter extinction; I leave behind only the Dharma-scriptures and flower garlands.
The ceremonial crown and jade pendants increase my grief as we assemble for the interment; the people mourn and the earth trembles, the sound of wailing how resonant!
The Vajra-mudrā staff appears in a dream from the Western Land, to signify that our Master has reached the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The Son of the Dharma King causes the ox-cart to startle and move forward; may he forever transcend birth and death and shatter the enmity of Māra.
The Abbot who received the Imperial Consecration from the Son of Heaven, A lineage transmitted through the sovereigns and the state, his origin at Gṛdhrakūṭa;
His reputation was like a dragon, his character like jade. With the *pātra* in hand, his gaze fixed upon the Sanskrit script;
His mind shared the brilliance of the white moon, its light reflecting in the azure pond. He shed his mortal skin and departed, his likeness painted in the Hall of the Qilin.

The three mysteries are silent and desolate; within the ninefold gates, grief and lamentation abound. As the *jiā* and *xiāo* pipes sound for the four-horse carriage, the journey extends ten thousand *lǐ*.
The clouds darken the heavens and the pines mourn across a thousand mountains. How can one bear to see this vast, azure world robbed of its Master?
Beholding his snow-white countenance, there is neither demonstration nor teaching; yet he has transmitted the vastness of kalpas—whence did he derive it? Whence did he receive it?

On the sixth day of the seventh month of the ninth year of the Dali era, the year being Jiayin (654), under the stem-branch combination of Wuxu and Gui-mao, an imperial decree was issued dispatching a court messenger to present this sacrificial text. The sacrificial text presented by the Imperial Envoy Liu Xianhe reads as follows: [The text continues with the formal invocation and offerings.]
The Emperor dispatched the Inner Attendant Liu Xianhe to respectfully offer incense, tea,
and libations as a sacrifice to the spirit of the late Tripitaka Master Dabianzheng Guangzhi.
Possessing a spiritual intellect and clear discernment, with a naturally sagacious disposition,
he had long cultivated pure conduct and possessed innate knowledge of the supreme causes.
Standing out as a preeminent figure throughout the Five Indias,
he traveled ten thousand *li*,
his mind containing the oceanic storehouse of the scriptures.
His fame reached both the Han and the Yi peoples;
he transmitted the sutras on palm leaves and expounded the teachings of the Yogācāra.
He brings vast benefit to the myriad people;
he appears and disappears at the three courts,
yet the Way resides in non-speaking.
In principle, all are uniform and traceless;
Nirvana is eternally quiescent,
and the ultimate sages all return to the same destination.
Incense was burned and the body was washed;
together with all things, it returns to extinction.
I, the Emperor, have received this definitive meaning.
The rites between teacher and disciple are complete;
at this moment of eternal parting, my grief is profound.
May the spirits of the offerings of incense and tea clearly perceive them.

A Memorial for the Day of the Funeral of Yuanxiang Gong, the Tripiṭaka Upādhyāya. One Memorial for the Day of the Funeral of Yuanxiang Gong. On the sixth day, the day of Kǒujiǎ, of the first month of the seventh lunar month in the year of Jiǎyín, the ninth year of the Dàlì era.
Yuan Zai, Vice Director of the Secretariat and concurrently Chief Consultant of the Chancellery,
reverently offers this sacrifice of incense and flowers to the spirit of the late Tripiṭaka Master, the Great Upādhyāya.
Alas! To dwell within a form and wander through transformations is like a wheel set in motion by the wind.
Though earth and water are vast, they all become my body;
yet the Perfected Person knows how to preserve them without clinging, entrusting them to the realm of quiescent extinction.
Having attained deliverance, he remained constantly weary of and detached from the dust of defiled craving.
Alas! The Great Master succeeded to the Buddha’s luminous cause;
his profound insight was all-encompassing and awakened.
His vast compassion meets with benevolence;
matter and mind are equally penetrated.
His merit and learning are ever renewed; our sovereign is luminously one with the Dao, attuned to it in profound harmony.
Virtue arises in due time;
the True Doctrine inaugurates its course,
awaiting succession in future generations.
Truly transmitting the secret seals,
they concentrated their minds in the quiet halls;
the Emperor descended from his carriage to extend his inquiries.
Facing east toward the honored teacher,
he advanced three steps with the wind at his back:
"May the Sage store up blessings."
The spirit is sustained and auspiciousness is met.
All of us, the fourfold assembly, have followed like clouds to this site of practice.
We now receive the final entrustment.
I look up to you as a bridge across the ford;
how could I ever fully repay your kindness?
Now that the ultimate source of our tradition has perished, what can be done?
Alas! The essence of the Dharma is perfectly illuminating throughout the limits of past and future;
it does not arise in dependence upon form, nor does it exist contingent upon the aggregation of conditions.
We gather once more at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa;
as the kalpas sit long before us,
we feel deep sorrow and longing for the divine countenance.
Forever cherishing the compassionate guidance, I humbly accept this grace.

A Memorial of Thanks for the Imperial Decree Bestowing the Posthumous Title of Minister of Works and a Posthumous Honorific Name; one memorial of thanks for the imperial decree bestowing the posthumous title and honorific name upon the late Master; and a response to the words of the śramaṇa Huilang and others from the wilderness.
On the evening of the sixth day of last month, when my late master was cremated,
Your Majesty’s sacred compassion moved by grief posthumously conferred upon him the rank of Minister of Works (Sikong).
He was further posthumously titled the Venerable Tripiṭaka Master Bukong of Great Eloquence, Rectitude,
and Vast Wisdom; thus national rites were proclaimed and the divine way was glorified.
The gifts bestowed by the Three Dukes have transcended former precedents;
the title "Harmonious Superior" (Heshang) has not been recorded in the classics of antiquity.
From this, we know the grace of the High Heavens.
Submerged in the rivers and seas without bound,
the numinous manifestations of the dark path shine down like the sun and moon;
there were several thousand disciples and many followers in total.
Moved by deep emotion and grateful for Your Majesty’s sacred grace,
I am overwhelmed with a sense of profound indebtedness.
I respectfully entrust this to the Imperial Messenger Li Xiancheng.
A memorial was respectfully submitted to express gratitude for imperial notice.
The śramaṇas Huilang and others, with utmost reverence and humility, state:

On the seventh day of the seventh month in the ninth year of the Dali era, the śramaṇas Huilang and others, currently serving as mere grass and soil at Daxingshan Monastery, submit this memorial to Emperor Baoying Yuansheng Wenwu. The Emperor’s decree: "The Venerable One originated his career in the Five Indias."
He traveled ten thousand *li*,
proclaiming and expounding the True Dharma to rescue and awaken all living beings.
Nirvana returns to the eternal;
filial conduct is honored with posthumous titles;
thus do the rites and classics endure.
I humbly express my gratitude for this favor.
Compiled by the Tripitaka Master of Great Eloquence, Correctness, and Vast Wisdom, under the Imperial Edict: Volume Four.
Presented during the Reign of Emperor Daizong; posthumously honored as Minister of Works (Sikong) by the Tripitaka Master of Great Eloquence, Correctness, and Vast Wisdom.
The Collected Imperial Edicts of the Upādhyāya, Volume Five.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Śīlarāja of Ximing Monastery in Chang’an, the Capital.
In total, twenty-nine pieces.

Answer: Sixteen edicts in total, comprising forty-five pieces: one edict for summoning monks for recitation; one edict for instructing the wise in the training of later students; one edict for ordering the wise to reside at Shengyi as requested;

one edict for halting the repair of the old stupa site; one edict for constructing a spirit-stupa within the current monastery; and a formal letter to the śramaṇa Huilang declining the gift of purple robes.

One memorial on robes representing the head [of the Sangha] and one imperial edict responding to the bestowal of the plaque for the Mañjuśrī Pavilion; one memorial of thanks for the bestowal of the plaque and one formal petition responding to the submission regarding the construction of the Great Sage Mañjuśrī State-Pacifying Pavilion;

one memorial of thanks for the gracious bestowal of offerings for the *xiang* (first anniversary) memorial service and one imperial edict responding to the disciple Huiguo’s thanks for the bestowal of silk and brocade;

and one imperial edict ordering monks and nuns throughout the realm to recite the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī* and one memorial of thanks for the recitation and upholding of the *Uṣṇīṣa-mantra*, along with one response to a request to act as a preceptor for the deceased.

One inscription for a stele by the Master; one memorial on the pacification of Li Lingyao; two verses in response to the elegies for the late Li Gong, Director of Merit; one memorial requesting the re-establishment of the Office of the Director of Merit;

one memorial of thanks for the bestowal of offerings for a vegetarian feast and tea; one memorial celebrating the spring snow; one response to the memorial celebrating the ordination of the Princess of Han;

one memorial by the monk Tanzhen of Qinglong Monastery thanking for gifts bestowed following prayers for rain; one response to the śramaṇa Feixi’s memorial celebrating fine weather; and one response to Jue.
One memorial by Seng Huichao on praying for rain at Chaohe Pool; one memorial in response to his request to decline service in the Inner Monastery;

one memorial by Seng Huichao on celebrating the prayer for rain; one memorial in response to Seng Huichao’s celebration of the defeat of the Tuoba; one memorial by Seng Tanzhen on celebrating the prayer for rain at Yumütan; one memorial in response to Seng Tanzhen’s celebration of the prayer for rain;
one memorial by Dao Run, a monk of Lingying Terrace, on celebrating the pacification of Henan; and one memorial presented by the Supervisor Xiancheng regarding the feathers of a frightened pigeon.
A Decree for Summoning Monks to Recite Mantras: One decree concerning the summoning of monks to recite mantras at Fenghua, Fudu, Baoshou, Xingshan, and other temples.
It concerns those monks who have rendered meritorious service by receiving the Dharma from the late Tripitaka Master.
The full title was then submitted for presentation.

On the seventh day of the seventh month in the ninth year of the Dali era, Li Xiancheng, Director of the Inner Attendants, proclaimed the imperial decree. **Imperial Decree: Bestowing the Title "Professor of Later Scholars" upon Hui-lang** One decree, issued by imperial command to the monk Hui-lang: [Text follows]
He was exclusively charged with overseeing the affairs of the monastery and concurrently instructing later generations of students;
he reported to the throne whenever there were matters concerning the single honored image or the single ritual covenant that followed the established sequence.

On the seventh day of the seventh month in the ninth year of the Dali era, Imperial Messenger Li Xiancheng proclaimed an edict: "In accordance with the request of the monk Huisheng, an imperial decree is issued to grant him a residence. This is one decree granted in accordance with the request of Huisheng. An imperial edict addressed to the monk Huisheng: [Text follows]
During the lifetime of our Upādhyāya,
Master Si was especially favored by him and received his full confidence;
now we hear that he has been burning incense and lamps at the stupa to offer protection.
Previously, you received the Samantabhadra Recitation Method from your preceptor;
it is held in equal esteem by me.
Strive with diligence in its cultivation for three years, and once that period is complete—
He immediately came before me to consult regarding the dharma of the Principal Deity (Honzon) and the site upon which he requested to reside.

On the seventh day of the seventh month in the ninth year of the Dali era, the Palace Attendant (Zhongshi Gaopin) Li Xiancheng proclaimed the imperial edict: "An Edict Regarding the Suspension of Repairs to the Site of the Old Stupa. One Edict, respectfully received by imperial decree, addressed to Yuancong."
Therefore, the construction of the stūpa for the Venerable Upādhyāya Tripitaka Master Bukong, the Great Distinguished and Correct One of Vast Wisdom, shall be temporarily suspended.
A separate site shall be selected and prepared for its construction.

On the fifteenth day of the seventh month in the ninth year of the Dali era, Imperial Messenger Li Xiancheng proclaimed an imperial edict at this monastery regarding the construction of the spirit-stūpa. One decree concerning the construction of the spirit-stūpa at this monastery, along with an official dispatch, was respectfully presented; by imperial command, it was addressed to Yuan Cong.
Therefore, it has been determined that the remains of the Tripiṭaka Master were cremated and śarīras were obtained;
an order is hereby issued to construct a śarīra stūpa at the temple where he resided.

On the twenty-eighth day of the eighth month in the ninth year of the Dali era, Li Xiancheng, Chief of the Inner Attendants (Nei-yeshi-jian), having proclaimed the imperial decree as the Commissioner for the Cultivation of Merit in Charge of the Temples and Observatories of the Capital, issues this notification to Xingshan Temple. The notification states that, in accordance with the decree as recorded above, no separate notifications have yet been sent to the relevant authorities regarding the implementation of these instructions. Consequently, the imperial decree is hereby recorded and notified to Xingshan Temple, and further notified to the former quarters of the late Tripiṭaka Upādhyāya. Thus notified.

The 8th day of the 9th month of the ninth year of the Dali era. Notification to the Assistant Official, the former Magistrate of Zizhou, Liu Hao; and to Li Cong, General of the Right Dragon Guard Army concurrently serving as Grand Master of Ceremonies with the same rank as a Minister of State. A Memorial by the Śramaṇa Huilang Thanking for the Bestowal of a Purple Robe. One memorial by the Śramaṇa Huilang thanking for the bestowal of a purple robe, together with a reply to the Śramaṇa Huilang.
I, Huilang, a most humble practitioner of Yoga,
have been graced by the imperial bounty and have unworthily received your extraordinary favor.
Entering and exiting the Golden Gate,
practicing austerities in a separate hall,
I have fortunately received Your Majesty’s clear decree.
Frequently appearing before the Ninefold Court,
he was specially granted the purple sash and the *kāṣāya* robe as an imperial favor;
this not only served to honor his late master with splendor, but...
This reality will surely illuminate future scholars;
I, a humble monk, am overcome with profound grief and respectfully submit this memorial to express my gratitude for your report.
I am overcome with the utmost anxiety and distress.
With sincere joy and delight, I respectfully submit these words.

On the twenty-ninth day of the eleventh month of the ninth year of the Dali era, the monk Huilang, a disciple who received the transmission of the Dharma from the late Tripitaka Master of Great Eloquence and Rectitude at Daxingshan Monastery, presented this memorial. Emperor Baoying Yuansheng Wenwu replied:
The Master had long been diligent in the holy life and was the first to tread upon the stream of the Dharma;
his realization was sustained by both merit and wisdom.
The living beings rely upon [your grace];
thus, you have been granted ceremonial robes.
I trouble you with these words of gratitude for your kindness.
Imperial Edict on the Bestowal of the Inscription for the Mañjuśrī Pavilion An Imperial Edict:
By imperial decree, the eight-part calligraphic inscription in golden script for the "Pavilion of the Great Sage Mañjuśrī, Guardian of the State" is hereby bestowed.
It is appropriate that this be sent to the Translation Hall of Daxingshan Temple.

On the thirteenth day of the second month in the tenth year of the Dali era, the Palace Messenger Li Xiancheng proclaimed [this decree]. A memorial of thanks for the bestowal of the temple name; one memorial of thanks for the bestowal of the temple name, spoken by the śramaṇa Huilang.
Today, I humbly received the imperial decree proclaimed by the Palace Messenger Li Xiancheng.
You were specially granted one plaque for the "Great Sage Mañjuśrī Hall," written in the Eight-Part Script (Bāfēn) with golden ink.
The divine traces of the Imperial Calligraphy are of extraordinary and peerless excellence.
Its name is "Majestic Guard of the Nation" (Xiongzheng Guo), and its characters are like "Candles of the Celestial Patterns.
The magpies glance back and the phoenixes wheel about, appearing as if they are truly in flight;
the dragon-like forms and martial postures stand far apart, transcending wind and clouds.
It casts the "hanging dew" [script] down from the nine heavens;
it causes the "falling stone" [script] to descend from the thousand-fathom heights.
Its golden light blazes forth, suspended together with the sun and moon; its sacred traces and exemplary models shall endure as imperishably as heaven and earth.
Beholding you in welcome and reverent gaze, my eyes are refreshed;
contemplating you with deep reflection and careful observation, my mind and spirit are clear and serene.
How fortunate this humble monk is to be bathed in such waves of grace!
Bearing this heavy burden upon my head, I am filled with shame before the high heavens and find no place to hide my humiliation.
Overwhelmed by the utmost joy and trepidation,
I respectfully submit this memorial to express my gratitude and bring it to Your Majesty’s ears.
The śramaṇa Huìlǎng expresses his sincere joy and gratitude.
Respectfully stated on the thirteenth day of the second month in the tenth year of the Dàlì era. Submitted by the śramaṇa Huìlǎng of Dàxīngshàn Temple. The Emperor Bǎoyìng Yuánshèng Wénwǔ replied:
The true likeness [of the Buddha] was enshrined in a separate courtyard of the monastery;
a golden plaque was displayed to manifest the glory of the Great Sage.
The Master diligently maintained the incense and lamps, protecting the state and the family.

The petition for leave to submit the memorial regarding the construction of the Great Sage Mañjuśrī State-Protection Pavilion is hereby acknowledged. Attached is one memorial regarding the construction of the Mañjuśrī Pavilion from the Translation Institute of Daxingshan Temple.
A pavilion for the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva was constructed,
with a total expenditure calculated at twenty-two thousand four hundred and eighty-seven strings and nine hundred and fifty cash.

The internal expenditure for silk substitutes totaled 13,502 strings of cash; of this, 11,152 strings were converted into 4,117 bolts of silk, while 2,000 strings were suppressed and 1,080 strings and 503 cash were entered as actual cash.
The sum of the upper robes, miscellaneous funds, and various items amounts to 8,355 guan and 447 wen.
This includes external offerings, various sundries, and proceeds from the sale of goods.
A pavilion for the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva should be constructed.
The expenditure and current inventory are as follows:
four thousand five hundred forty-two strings and five hundred forty-five cash.
Six hundred ten and a half pieces of oak were purchased for nine hundred seventy-four thousand eight hundred ten cash.
Eight hundred four rafters, columns, and locust-wood beams were purchased in total.
One thousand four hundred and ninety-one strings and one hundred seventy cash.
Purchased fifty-five thousand six hundred and ninety-eight bricks, tiles, and *zhishou* (mythical roof-riders).
Two hundred fourteen thousand five hundred *wen* were used for the purchase of seven hundred bundles of straw and other expenses.
Seven hundred forty-six thousand two hundred twenty-five *wen*.
Seven hundred and sixty-four thousand coins were spent on purchasing cypress wood for the construction of doors, windows, railings, and other such items;

seven hundred and sixty-four thousand coins were spent on purchasing stone anchors and various miscellaneous stones, as well as hiring carts, manual laborers, and providing them with food and provisions.
One hundred sixteen thousand four hundred twenty-five coins were used for the purchase of hemp,
*mātuluṅga*, and other items.
Three hundred thirty-nine thousand five hundred ninety-one coins [were used for other purposes].
Eighty thousand coins were used for items such as nails and iron;
eighty thousand were used for the construction of two stories for the pavilion and eight kites, among other things.
Eighty-five thousand two hundred and eighty-eight *wen* were spent on purchasing lime,
red earth, black wax, and other materials.
Two thousand four hundred and seventy-eight *guan* and nine hundred and forty-six *wen* were expended.
The cost for casting gold and copper nails, door-knockers,
various fittings, and tools amounted to 694,550 cash.
The cost for hiring laborers to construct steps and remove the moat amounted to [the same].
Two thousand two hundred and eighty-eight strings and three hundred cash.
Eight hundred strings for hiring laborers, erecting the wooden pillars,
and expenses for manual labor and provisions.
Purchased pigments, silk for unraveling borders, gauze-patterned fabrics, soft materials for handiwork, grain, and other necessities:
one thousand fifty-one strings and two hundred ninety-six cash.
The cost for hiring laborers to fell timber, including wages and provisions,
