is three thousand five hundred wen.
The cost for hiring laborers to construct tile-roofed houses, including wages and provisions, is as follows.
One thousand five hundred and eighteen *kuan* and nine hundred *wen*.
Three hundred and thirty *kuan* were used for the construction of the cypress gate, windows, railings,
sunshades, manual labor, food, and other provisions.
Two hundred and fifty-seven strings of cash were used for the labor and provisions for constructing the mud walls;
two hundred and fifty-seven strings of cash were used for hiring people to draw the mountain ridges,
foundations, and partitions, as well as for purchasing pigments and the labor and provisions required for these tasks.
Five hundred ninety-five thousand six hundred eighty-seven *wen* for the purchase of timber;
three hundred fifty-seven thousand seven hundred *wen* for hiring laborers, carts, boats, and carriage fees.
Expenses for hiring laborers to lay bricks and build structures,
including wages and provisions, amounted to 162,548 wen. Expenses for purchasing bamboo mats,
straw mats, reed screens, charcoal, medicinal flowers, hoes, paper, brushes, oil, and other supplies amounted to [the same].
One hundred guan and nine hundred eighty-two wen.
For the expenses of the monastic attendants, external messengers, the procurement of grain, and the laborers for construction:
fifty-two guan and five hundred ten wen.
Expenses for purchasing glue, hemp, rope, and various other sundries amounted to 312,790 coins.
Expenses for hiring miscellaneous laborers,
including monthly and daily wages, amounted to [the same amount].
Eight hundred seventy-three strings and two hundred fifty cash were used for the purchase of four carriages, six oxen, and other items;
six hundred eighty-two strings and eighty-seven cash [remained].
[These funds were] used for purchasing grass and beans for the oxen, medicine for the oxen, travel expenses, and money for cakes;
the detailed breakdown of expenditures is as previously stated. The items to be purchased, those included in miscellaneous offerings, those diverted, and the remaining balance are as follows:
A total of six hundred and eighty-five and a half square wooden beams were incorporated; of these, seven hundred and fifty beams were added externally, making six hundred and ten and a half.
Four hundred and eighty-seven and a half beams were purchased; one hundred and twenty-seven beams were consumed in the construction of the pavilion; seventy-one beams remain in stock.
A total of two hundred and forty-four pillars were joined and inserted: one hundred and forty-eight were externally applied and inserted;
one hundred and seventy-three were purchased and used for the construction of the pavilion; seventy-one remain in stock.

A total of two thousand four hundred and fourteen rafters were installed: one thousand five hundred and seventy were set within the main structure, and eight hundred and forty-four were applied externally.
One thousand eight hundred and fifty-four bundles were purchased; five hundred and sixty bundles have been used for the construction of the pavilion, and five hundred and sixty bundles remain.

A total of seven hundred bundles of timber were purchased for the construction of the storehouse; three hundred and fifty bundles have been used for the construction of the pavilion, and three hundred and fifty bundles remain.

A total of six hundred and eighty-three *jin* of glue were incorporated: six hundred *jin* were supplied by imperial decree; forty *jin* were contributed by external donors; and forty-three *jin* were purchased for use in the construction of the pavilion. Once completed, [the materials] were accounted for.
A total of six hundred and twenty *jin* of wax was entered [into the records]: six hundred *jin* by imperial decree and twenty *jin* purchased. All were used up for the construction of the pavilion.

The above details—including the money and materials such as square timber and various miscellaneous expenses entered for the construction of the pavilion, as well as the quantities currently remaining—are recorded here as previously stated. We respectfully submit this for Your Majesty’s perusal and await Your Imperial Decree.
Memorial submitted on the fifth day of the fourth month in the tenth year of the Dali era by the supervising monk Xiu Yan and others in charge of the construction of the pavilion,
together with the supervising monk Hui Sheng.
Imperial decree to the supervising monk Hui Lang in charge of the affairs of the monastery.

A Memorial of Thanks for the Imperial Bestowal of a Memorial Feast for the First Anniversary of the Funeral (Xiaoxiang). One memorial of thanks for the imperial bestowal of a memorial feast for the first anniversary of the funeral, together with a response to the Imperial Messenger Duan Wuhua, who arrived to proclaim the Sacred Edict.
In commemoration of the first anniversary of the interment of the Great Master Tripitaka Śramaṇa of Great Eloquence, Rectitude, and Vast Wisdom, one thousand people were granted a vegetarian feast,
two hundred strings of tea were bestowed, and two disciples were ordained.
I humbly observe that since our late Master entered nirvana,
a full cycle of years has passed; yet Your Majesty’s sagely thoughts have continued to honor his final resting place with successive acts of imperial grace.
He was granted funds to erect a stupa and bestowed offerings and ordinations upon monks; thus,
the grace of rain and dew reached both the hidden and the manifest realms.
His radiant grace extends to both the living and the deceased;
all those within the ranks of the Dharma community are moved by a mingling of sorrow and shame.
Imperial envoys arrived in succession;
incense and tea followed one after another,
as he was escorted to the body of the Prabhūtaratna Buddha.
Having received extraordinary grace from the Nine Heavens,
I am overwhelmed with the utmost sense of gratitude and veneration.
I respectfully submit this memorial to express my thanks for Your Majesty’s knowledge.
I am overcome with the utmost anxiety and distress.
With sincere joy and delight, I respectfully submit this message.

On the fifteenth day of the sixth month in the tenth year of the Dali era, the śramaṇa Huilang of Daxingshan Temple presented this memorial. The Emperor, the Most Venerable, Holy, Sage, Martial, and Civilly Refined, replied as follows:
Our former Upādhyāya has entered parinirvāṇa and returned to the eternal;
as the succession of the stars has suddenly shifted,
my grief and lamentation increase all the more.
In honoring and exalting blessings and protection,
and providing the requisites for the fast and offerings,
I consider this no small measure of generous support.
I trouble you with this expression of thanks.
Disciple Huiguo’s memorial of thanks for the bestowed silk and brocade; one memorial of thanks for the imperial gift of silk and brocade, together with a reply to the śramaṇa Huiguo.
I have humbly received the imperial decree proclaimed by the Central Envoy Li Xiancheng on the ninth day of this month,
graciously bestowing upon this humble monk twenty bolts of brocade and silk.
As I receive and contemplate these gifts, my joy and trepidation are as great as a mountain pressing down upon me.
I, Huiguo, am fortunate to have encountered this era of peace and brilliance,
and have humbly received the imperial bounty;
since the age when I gathered grains of sand, I have served my former master.
For more than twenty years, he has upheld the staff and water-strainer,
[upholding] the esoteric school of Yoga and the profound and subtle essentials of Samantabhadra.
I have been especially favored by your instructions and have fully received your intent;
you have earnestly commanded me to practice day and night for the sake of the nation.
For this reason, the humble monks have shattered their hearts and exhausted their livers, casting aside their forms and sacrificing their lives without a moment’s interruption.
With such earnest vows and sincerity, they seek to repay the grace of the rain and dew.
I hope to repay this extraordinary act of private grace.
Overwhelmed by the utmost joy and exultation,
I respectfully submit this memorial to express my gratitude for Your Majesty’s knowledge.
I, the śramaṇa Huiguo, speak with both sincere joy and trepidation.

On the tenth day of the eleventh month of the tenth year of the Dali era, this memorial is respectfully submitted by the śramaṇa Huiguo of Daxingshan Monastery to His Majesty Emperor Baoying Yuansheng Wenwu. [The Emperor’s] Imperial Response: The Bequeathed Teachings of the Upādhyāya.
The Ācārya strictly adhered to the secret tradition and transmitted it to his disciples;
having perused the Master’s earnest memorial expressing his diligent toil, [he was deeply moved].
I have used thin tin and silk scrolls to honor the incense and lamps; may you be aware of this.
Thank you for your understanding.

Imperial Edict for Monks and Nuns Throughout the Realm to Recite the Mantra of the Dhāraṇī of the Exalted Victorious One. An Imperial Decree for the Monks and Nuns Throughout the Realm to Recite the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī*. One copy of this decree was respectfully presented in accordance with the imperial instructions to Li Yuancong.
All monks and nuns throughout the empire shall be ordered to recite the Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī.
They shall be required to master it thoroughly within the course of one month,
and furthermore, they must recite it twenty-one times every day.
Every year on the first day of the first month,
an envoy to offer New Year’s congratulations was dispatched to present the number of recitations performed.

On the eighth day of the second month in the eleventh year of the Dali era, Li Xiancheng, Director of the Inner Attendants, announced the following: A memorial of thanks for the recitation and retention of the Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī, one piece; together with a reply to the śramaṇa Huìlǎng.
I have humbly received the gracious imperial decree ordering that all monks and nuns throughout the empire shall recite and uphold the *Buddhōṣṇīṣa-vijaya-dhāraṇī*,
the eye and mind of all Buddhas.
A bridge and raft for the common people— Your Majesty has received the Buddha’s entrustment and extends his transformative teachings through the Dharma.
Your gracious brilliance shines forth within the monastic community.
Furthermore, having received the privilege of serving as a close attendant,
my humble sincerity is filled with both profound awe and great joy.
I humbly beseech Your Majesty to ensure that your deliberations are in perfect harmony with your sagely compassion.
To secretly assist in generating benefit and lead others to the realm of benevolence and longevity depends upon these few words.
He spreads far-reaching glory to bring peace to the myriad states;
even the spirits of the mountains and rivers find tranquility.
Birds, beasts, fish, and turtles will truly receive blessings;
the Sangha will have a path for advancement,
and the secular world will achieve a climate of shared virtue.
This, then, is Your Majesty’s transcendent grace toward all under heaven;
that you take up and employ the Ultimate Way—
how could it be something known through the daily activities of an ignorant monk?
The grace of your life-sustaining nourishment is profound and deep;
as for the virtue of your instruction and guidance, by what means can I adequately repay it?
I respectfully submit this memorial of thanks through the Imperial Messenger Yuan Yingjin to inform Your Majesty.
With sincere joy and delight, we respectfully submit these words.

On the twenty-third day of the second month of the eleventh year of the Dali era, the Śramaṇas Huilang and others of Xingshan Monastery presented this memorial concerning the "Buddhapiṭaka-mantra" (Fo ding zhen yan) of the Emperor, the Greatly Responsive, Primordial Sage, Martial and Civilly Refined August Emperor; [the Emperor] then issued his decree.
May its divine power extend widely,
providing ample support for great benefit and reaching all sentient beings.
I have recently ordered you to recite and uphold [this text];
I hereby express my gratitude for your diligent efforts.
We request that you compose an inscription for a stele in honor of our late master. One Inscription for a Stele in Honor of Our Late Master, by the Śramaṇas Huìlǎng and others, states:
Our late master, the Great Venerable Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra,
early encountered this sagely age and succeeded to the Buddha’s transmission of the lamp.
Crossing the seas and climbing mountains,
he sought the treasure of the Dharma and obtained the Vajra-seal of Esoteric Truth.
Having realized samādhi and dhāraṇī,
the śarīra is enshrined within the physical body,
and the mirror of wisdom is suspended in the moon of the mind.
He leveled the Great Way and assisted the Imperial House. Since the Tianbao era,
our imperial ancestors and our late imperial father have humbled their majesty to inquire about the Dharma.
The rites between teacher and disciple are fully established;
Your Majesty, presiding over the court, further adds exceptional honor,
revering their virtue and character.
His honors and gifts surpassed those of his peers;
while alive, he was titled the "Consecrated Master," and upon his death,
he was posthumously granted the rank of Upper Duke.
Since his passing into nirvana,
years have passed;
yet the shadow stupa stands empty within the twin śāla trees.
His magnificent virtue has not yet been inscribed upon the enduring stone; out of sacred compassion and affectionate concern, Your Majesty has granted permission to fashion a grand monument.
Beholding this celestial inscription, we hope that he will descend and abide therein.
This humble monk’s long-cherished vow is now nearing its fulfillment.
I prostrate myself and beseech Your Majesty’s vast grace to look upon me with compassion and grant my request.
I am overwhelmed by the utmost sincerity of my plea.
We respectfully present this memorial to submit our petition for Your Majesty’s consideration.
Having presumptuously intruded upon Your Imperial Majesty’s presence, we are overcome with trepidation and fear.
The śramaṇas Huilang and others, in all humility and awe, speak thus.

On the fifth day of the fourth month in the eleventh year of the Dali era, the śramaṇas Huilang and others of Daxingshan Monastery presented this memorial to congratulate on the pacification of Li Lingyao. Memorial of the Śramaṇas Huilang and Others Congratulating on the Pacification of Li Lingyao: The śramaṇas Huilang and others state: [...]
Upon hearing this, Huilang [thought]:
"One who opposes virtue will surely perish; a calamity arising from one's own offspring is difficult to evade.
I humbly beseech Your Majesty to exercise sagely wisdom and make a decisive judgment."
He secretly employed divine stratagems and utilized the martial prowess of his generals and soldiers; with sincere devotion, he suppressed the rebels,
capturing the enemy chieftains with swift success.
The eight provinces having been secured, overseas routes were opened;
the ten thousand nations came to court,
and the four barbarian tribes presented tribute.
Śramaṇas Huìlǎng and others, overcome with the utmost joy and delight,
respectfully submit this memorial along with Imperial Messenger Lǐ Xiàochéng to announce our congratulations.
Śramaṇas Huìlǎng and others, truly joyful and delighted, respectfully state.

On the twenty-eighth day of the eleventh month in the eleventh year of the Dali era, the śramaṇas Huilang and others of Daxingshan Monastery presented a memorial to the Emperor, the One of Precious Response, the Primordial Sage, the Martial and Civilly Virtuous. The Emperor replied as follows:
The brilliant star rebelled in madness, defying the imperial edicts;
when the military commanders arrived from the four directions,
the rebels were shattered like mist at dawn.
The ringleader of the rebellion has been captured.
Bianzhou is on the verge of recovering its former prosperity.
I am aware of this cause for celebration.
Eulogies for the Late General Li, Duke of Liang, Former Commissioner of Merit; two poems by Zhao Qian, former Military Counselor of the Left Commandery Guard and Palace Attendant.
His meritorious deeds flourished during the era of Yao;
his achievements were perfected at the court of King Wen’s son.
He has repeatedly received the favor of three emperors.
The six ministers' merits are compared to the five notes;
the painted horns sigh with a cold blast,
and the sorrowful *jia* reed pipes choke on the dawn clouds— the bones of loyalty and righteousness in the Sage Dynasty.
Today I visit this desolate grave;
from the great tree, a mournful wind arises.
The General has departed and will not return.
Touching the coffin, my heart grows ever more pained;
facing the grave pit, my tears are hard to restrain.
The morning moon shines upon the heavy frost and the grass.
The dark spring conceals the night tomb;
again I hear the lamentation of singing companions.
Stirred by every object, all has become sorrow.
Petition for the Continued Appointment of the Official for Merit (Gongde Shi) A Petition for the Continued Appointment of the Official for Merit, composed by the Śramaṇa Huilang:
Huilang humbly states: I have heard that when humans plant blessings, [the merit is inexhaustible].
Truly, it is for the benefit of all people;
were its office not established, virtue would have no means to flourish.
We humbly beseech Your Majesty, the Emperor Baoying Yuansheng Wenwu.
That which he ascended was the heavenly mandate;
it was surely for the sake of the common people,
to block off and sever the paths of heterodoxy.
By upholding the True Dharma,
all nations are blessed;
how much more so the capital city, ever since the State specifically established the Office of Merit and Virtue.
The multitude of blessings increases daily;
the host of evils is extinguished from time to time.
The Imperial House receives exalted protection, and the community of monastics is forever freed from the peril of humiliation—this is known only to Heaven.
Few people have realized this.
Yesterday, when Yuancong passed away,
the monastics of the imperial capital looked upon one another with somber countenances.
Raising my eyes, my grief increased;
as I spoke these words, tears fell from my eyes.
Furthermore, I feared that the evil Māra would find an opportunity to seize my mind.
The heretics have found their opportunity to bared-arms;
the True Teaching declines while the forest of heterodoxy flourishes.
I humbly entreat Your Majesty’s compassionate grace to select a worthy minister to oversee the office of merit,
thereby ensuring the eternal blessings of renewal for the state.
To alleviate the sorrow of the monk’s nostalgia for his homeland,
I respectfully entrust this memorial of thanks to the Surveillance Commissioner, Yi Hwon-ch’ŏng, to be presented for Your Majesty’s consideration.
I am overcome with the utmost sense of trepidation.
The Śramaṇa Huìlǎng, with utmost reverence and trepidation, respectfully addresses these words.

On the [blank] day of the twelfth month of the eleventh year of the Dàlì era, the Śramaṇa Huìlǎng of Dàxīngshàn Monastery submits this memorial to thank for the imperial gift of vegetarian provisions and tea. One Memorial Submitted by the Śramaṇa Huìlǎng to Thank for the Gift of Vegetarian Provisions and Tea. The Śramaṇa Huìlǎng says:
I have humbly received the imperial decree of the fourteenth day of this month, ordering the preparation of a vegetarian feast for one thousand monks and the bestowal of two hundred strings of tea.
Today, I have again been graced by the arrival of an imperial messenger who proclaimed Your Majesty’s gracious command.
He consoled his disciples;
the celestial fragrance spread everywhere,
perfuming both the living and the deceased.
Huilang and the others are truly grieved and terrified;
our spirits are shattered and our souls in turmoil.
We rely upon the lingering shade of our late master’s legacy.
Having bathed in Your Majesty’s extraordinary grace,
should there be any truth in the divine principle,
may I receive a hidden response to this holy bounty.
Thus, the requital of the "binding of grass" must surely have originated from this fragrant tea.
I am overwhelmed by a sense of profound indebtedness, as vast as the mountains and seas.
I respectfully enclose this memorial with the Imperial Messenger Li Xiancheng to present my expressions of gratitude for Your Majesty’s knowledge.
The śramaṇa Huìlǎng, with utmost reverence and trepidation, respectfully addresses these words.

On the tenth day of the sixth month of the twelfth year of the Dàlì era, the śramaṇas Huìlǎng and others submit this memorial to offer congratulations on the spring snow. This is one memorial for congratulating on the spring snow. The śramaṇas Huìlǎng and others state:
Recently, during last winter, excessive warmth prevailed, causing Your Majesty’s heart to be filled with anxiety and concern;
you have extensively cultivated supreme merit for the sake of all living beings.
As a result, spring clouds drench the sky and pure white snow reveals its beauty;
the heavens everywhere hold moisture,
and its bounty extends without limit.
The turbid dust shall naturally clear,
and a bountiful year may be awaited.
[This was done by] fifty-three monks, including Huirang and others.
Whenever he was at the site of practice,
he would recite [the mantra] for the sake of the state;
this has been so since the beginning of the Zhengsheng era.
They exhorted one another;
some did not eat for seven days,
while others remained awake for ten days without sleeping.
Valuing even a fragment of merit,
he responds to Your Majesty’s extraordinary grace;
he bathes in the benevolence of the Yao era.
I remain ashamed before the rustic elders and am filled with the utmost joy.
I respectfully submit this memorial to convey my congratulations, accompanying it with the Imperial Messenger Li Xiancheng for Your Majesty’s perusal.
The śramaṇas Huìlǎng and others, filled with sincere joy and gladness, respectfully submit this statement.
On the seventeenth day of the first month of the thirteenth year of the Dàlì era.
The śramaṇas Huìlǎng and others of Dàxīngshàn Monastery present this memorial to the Emperor, the One of Precious Response, the Primordial Sage, the Martial and Civilly Wise. The Emperor replied:
Recently, as it was time for the sprouting of new growth yet there had been no snow since winter,
my heart was deeply concerned with the year's harvest and distressed by the lingering heat.
Your Eminence’s prayers were performed with the utmost sincerity.
The balm of grace has been universally bestowed;
moved by your utmost sincerity,
you should find comfort therein.
We respectfully submit this memorial.

A Memorial on the Ordination of the Princess of Hanwang, one scroll. Submitted by the assembly of the Buddhist community at Daxingshan Monastery in the capital, headed by the Chief Monk (Upādhyāya) Śramaṇa Huilang and others: [The text continues with the formal address and petition.]
I have reverently received the Imperial Edict of the sixth day of this month, granting the ordination of the eldest daughter of the Great King of Korea.
By this vast grace, the Heavenly Grandchild is permitted to leave the household life; may the Empress follow in her footsteps, continuing the radiant favor bestowed upon the Śākya lineage.
I humbly reflect that Your Majesty’s most sagacious mind benefits all things with vast magnanimity;
though as great as heaven and earth, who could possibly serve as its metaphor?
Setting aside the phoenix-patterned hairpins of the *chánbìn* hairstyle, they shaved their cloud-like tresses;
casting off jeweled robes and necklaces, they donned the *kāṣāya*.
Thus, all beings within the three realms—humans and devas alike—were bathed in the blessings and grace [of this merit].
The monastic community throughout the world cannot sufficiently express its gratitude and congratulations.
We respectfully submit this memorial through the imperial messenger Wei Xinglin for Your Majesty’s perusal.
The śramaṇas Huilang and others, filled with sincere joy and delight, respectfully submit this statement.

On the ninth day of the tenth month in the thirteenth year of the Dali era, the *śramaṇa* Huilang, the *upādhyāya* of the Great Xingshan Monastery in the capital, and others submitted a memorial; [this is followed by] the *śramaṇa* Tanzhen’s memorial congratulating [the Emperor] on the bestowal of gifts for praying for rain at Qinglong Monastery, and his single memorial congratulating [the Emperor] on the bestowal of gifts for praying for rain at Nanshan, along with the Imperial Response to the *śramaṇa* Tanzhen.
Recently, as the life-giving rains have not yet fallen, Your Majesty’s heart has been filled with anxiety and concern.
You have specifically issued an edict ordering me to go to the Southern Mountains to pray for rain.
With liver and gall exhausted,
I hope to attain the Heavenly Mind;
yet regarding the Dharma, I have achieved no merit.
The dragon deities did not respond;
your sagely reflections were toiled in vain,
and your provisions were spent in vain.
Since there is no prospect of joy,
I truly deserve punishment and reproach; yet Your Majesty’s compassionate grace has been so magnanimous as to bestow such profound bounty.
I have been granted seventy rolls of fine silk; yet,
though I wear the sky above and tread upon the earth below,
I do not know their height or thickness.
How could I have expected that at this gate of sorrow and indignation, I would suddenly encounter the Sage and receive his all-pervading grace?
I am overwhelmed by the utmost joy, jubilation, shame, and trepidation.
I respectfully entrust this memorial of thanks to the Imperial Messenger Li Xiancheng to present for Your Majesty’s perusal.
The Śramaṇa Tánzhēn, with utmost reverence and joy, respectfully addresses Your Majesty.

On the third day of the eighth month of the twelfth year of the Dàlì era, the Śramaṇa Tánzhēn of Qīnglóng Monastery presents this memorial to the Emperor, the One of Precious Response, the Primordial Sage, the Martial and Civilly Wise. The Emperor replied:

The Master has long exerted himself in the Brahma-faring and early on established a reputation for his sincerity, piety, and purity. He has prayed most earnestly at the site of practice (*dōjō*) for a bountiful rain; thus, I humbly offer this meager token of reward and present these words of thanks.
A Memorial of Congratulations on Clear Weather by the Śramaṇa Feixi; one memorial of congratulations on clear weather, together with the reply to the Śramaṇas Feixi and others.
I have humbly received the imperial decree proclaimed on the twenty-sixth day of the eighth month by the Imperial Messenger, the High-Ranking Official Li Xiancheng,
ordering the assembly of the Śramaṇa community in all the monasteries of the capital to recite the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, the Mahāmāyūrī Vidyārājñī Sūtra, and other scriptures.
He diligently exerted himself to stop the rain,
thereby fulfilling the Sage’s intention;
this was heard by Feixi.
Even the most sagely Emperor Yao was not without excessive rain;
the *Mahāmegha Sūtra* likewise records the transformation of requesting its cessation.
Lately, it has been somewhat like this persistent downpour.
While Your Majesty personally exposed your heart to the Jin people, confiding your anxieties within the moats,
you burned incense daily in the Jade Hall.
Consequently, the clear light ascended, piercing through the heavy clouds to shine in all directions.
The benevolent wind vibrates far and wide, sweeping away the mists and vapors from the eight directions.
The offerings of grain may be expected,
and the granaries shall forever overflow.
All of this is due to the Emperor’s compassionate and profound devotion;
how could the monastics know of it?
All those among both the clergy and the laity feel an overwhelming sense of gratitude.
I respectfully submit this memorial through the imperial envoy Li Xiancheng to announce my congratulations.
The śramaṇas Feixi and others are truly joyful and elated; they respectfully state.

On the first day of the ninth month of the twelfth year of Dali, the assembly of śramaṇas from the Buddhist community in the capital, led by Feixi, presents this memorial. The Emperor, the One of Precious Response, the Primordial Sage, Martial and Civil, replied:
The Master was a leader of the monastic community;
having long resided at the site of practice,
he diligently cultivated karmic conditions for the Dharma.
Blessings shall sustain the common people;
truly sanctified by divine protection,
their latent merit gradually unfolds.
It is fitting that you increase your reverent sincerity, so that blessings may flow upon both the family and the state.
I acknowledge your congratulations.
A Memorial for Prayer for Rain at Hejiu Lake by the Śramaṇa Juechao and others. The Śramaṇas Juechao, Huizhao, and others state: [The memorial follows.]

On the fifteenth day of this month, the imperial envoy Yang Guibin arrived and respectfully conveyed the Sacred Edict, ordering Juechao and others to pray for rain at the Nanshan reservoir for seven days. Your Majesty, with reverent self-discipline, nurtures all creatures.
He contemplated the sweet rains at their proper time,
taking the people as his own heart;
he took pity on the farmers' cultivation as they awaited a bountiful harvest.
Consequently, those with spiritual sensitivity surely offer prayers, and divine traces are attained through supplication;
thus, the myriad people receive the grace of compassionate love,
and all living beings rejoice in the righteousness of parental care.
Recently, although rain has fallen sparingly, all the hundred grasses flourish;
there is no cause for anxiety regarding drought, as the five grains all thrive.
This is surely due to Your Majesty’s subtle operation of the Way in accordance with Heaven.
The transformation of the fundamental source brings harmony within;
our awakening surpasses that of the common masses, yet we remain as ignorant as ever—we cannot bear the extreme weight of this auspicious excellence.
All people possess consciousness.
How could this surpass the height of our joy and devotion?
Having awakened to and humbly received the Imperial Decree,
we have immediately established a *dharmāśraya* (place of practice).
Day and night, with utmost sincerity,
they strove to fulfill the Emperor’s enlightened intentions,
not daring to be remiss.
To manifest the glorious reign of the enlightened era,
he recited the first scripture for one night;
suddenly, clouds and mist enveloped the mountains and rivers.
Before two days had passed since the petition was made,
a copious rain suddenly fell upon the city gates;
thus one knows this to be a response to the prayers of Yao’s era.
The profound response lies in a mere moment;
regarding the deliberations of the "Sun of Shun," auspicious omens will no longer be delayed.
The crops that have been planted suddenly seem as if they have been enriched with oil;
all that is called grain stores [shall likewise flourish].
Truly, he was about to surpass even the lowliest;
his awakening transcended that of the village elders and common folk,
who all wore him upon their heads and leaped for joy.
Unconsciously, his hands began to dance amidst the lanes and hamlets;
he splashed about and then stopped,
naturally beginning to tread with his feet upon the thoroughfares and alleys.
We cannot contain our boundless joy and exultation.
We respectfully submit this memorial to announce our congratulations.
The śramaṇas Juechao, Huizhao, and others, filled with sincere delight and joy, respectfully state:

On the twentieth day of the sixth month in the seventh year of the Dali era, the śramaṇas Juechao, Huiran, and others of Baoshou Monastery submitted a memorial. Emperor Baoying Yuansheng Wenwu replied:
The Master and his disciples practiced walking meditation and sat in quietude;
after long discourse on non-arising,
their thoughts turned deeply toward their homeland.
I sincerely pray for the descent of your gracious dew;
may the Holy and True One grant his protection.
May the falling rain respond to its appointed time.
The autumn plains are filled with abundance;
wearing honor, we enjoy the auspicious grain.
We look forward to a bountiful harvest at the end of the year.
I am grateful for your diligent efforts;
I understand your congratulations.

A Memorial Requesting Leave from the Inner Daochang, composed by the śramaṇas Juechao, Huikai, and others of the Changsheng Palace Daochang, states as follows: The śramaṇas Juechao, Huikai, and others of the Changsheng Palace Daochang address this memorial to Your Majesty: [text continues]
Juechao, Huihai, and others had no prior record of virtuous conduct or achievement,
yet they were indiscriminately admitted into the ranks of the monastic community to attend upon their late master.
He entered and exited the inner palace;
his meals were reduced to the imperial fare;
and his clothing was diminished from celestial robes.
For more than fifteen years, he has followed the routine of coming and going by carriage, like a horse in a stable.
His extraordinary private favors have accumulated like a mountain;
his meritorious service in repaying the state is beyond measure.
Not even a speck of dust has been achieved;
reflecting upon my own limited progress,
how can I bear the shame and remorse?
Furthermore, those who have left the household life receive the instructions of the Buddha;
they should diligently cultivate merit and reside within a monastery.
Having long resided in the celestial palaces,
this has indeed invited public censure;
I have reflected upon this day and night.
How can our hearts find peace?
We specially entreat Your Sacred Majesty’s compassion to grant us clemency and release,
so that we may each return to our respective temples.
Practicing for the sake of the nation is sustained by the field of merit;
how could it be restricted to either the inner or outer realms?
With the utmost sincerity and reverence, we respectfully enclose this memorial,
presented through Imperial Messenger Li Xiancheng, to submit our petition for Your Majesty’s consideration.
We, the śramaṇas Juechao, Huikai, and others, prostrate ourselves in profound awe and trepidation, and humbly submit this statement.

On the twenty-second day of the fifth month in the twelfth year of the Dali era, the recitation monks Juechao, Huikai, and others presented a memorial to the Emperor, the Greatly Responsive, Primordial Sage, Martial and Civilly Wise. The Emperor replied as follows:
The Master and his disciples cultivated sublime conduct with diligent effort,
firmly upholding the True Enlightenment while remaining within the inner palace.
Employing vast and superior causes,
there is neither going nor coming;
why then resort to such formalities of yielding?
A Memorial on the Occasion of Praying for Rain; one memorial on praying for rain, together with a response to the words of the śramaṇa Juechao and others.
I have humbly received the imperial decree proclaimed by the Palace Messenger Wei Xinglin on the twenty-seventh day of the eighth month.
When the long-persisting rain suddenly ceased at the command of the Emperor,
Juechao and the others were moved to redouble their reverent devotion upon receiving the imperial decree.
I address the dragon deities:
day and night I have been sincere and earnest,
exhausting every fiber of my liver and gallbladder.
By virtue of Your Majesty’s celestial majesty,
the clouds have dispersed and the rain has ceased;
the autumn crops all flourish with abundant fruit.
I humbly submit that the Emperor’s sagely virtue moves Heaven;
he nurtures all creatures like his own children,
and throughout the realm, hearts are filled with joy.
All the officials rejoice.
The monks of the ritual site are overcome with the utmost joy.
We respectfully submit this memorial through the Imperial Messenger, Music Director Qin, to offer our congratulations and report the news.
The śramaṇas Juechao and others, filled with sincere joy and gladness, respectfully submit this statement.

On the first day of the ninth month of the twelfth year of the Dali era, at the Daochang in Changsheng Palace, the śramaṇas Juechao and others presented this memorial to the Emperor, the Most Precious Response, the Primordial Sage, the Martial and Civilly Wise. The Emperor replied:
The Master was a leader of the monastic community;
having long resided at the site of practice,
he diligently cultivated karmic conditions for the Dharma.
Blessings shall support the common people;
truly, they are protected by the Sage.
As past merit gradually unfolds, [the path] becomes clear.
It is fitting that you increase your sincerity, so that blessings may flow upon the state and the family.
I acknowledge your congratulations.
This is one memorial congratulating the defeat of the Tufan, along with the response to the śramaṇas Juechao and others.
I have humbly observed the official dispatch announcing that General Li Baoyi’s subordinate officers and soldiers have defeated the Tubo,
capturing several thousand living prisoners and beheading over ten thousand enemies.
I have humbly heard that when one punishes the rebellious in accordance with what is right,
the mobilization of troops will surely achieve success;
when one restrains excess through righteousness, victory is certain.
There was nothing he undertook that he did not achieve.
Recently, however, the barbarian hordes have violated their covenant and dared to betray the grace of our state.
From the frontiers of the military borders,
we rely upon the rocky terrain.
We humbly reflect that Your Majesty’s sagely strategy penetrates the divine, and Your Celestial威 (awe) resounds far and wide.
The momentum was like splitting bamboo;
it was like fire consuming the plains.
The leaders were captured, and corpses filled the fields.
We, Juechao and others, being unworthy members of the Śākya school,
rejoice that the course of the state has been purified;
we cannot contain our utmost joy and exultation.
We respectfully present this memorial to offer our congratulations for your perusal.
The śramaṇas Juechao and others, filled with sincere joy and delight, respectfully submit this.

On the twenty-eighth day of the eighth month in the twelfth year of the Dali era, the śramaṇas Juechao and others of Baoshou Monastery within the Inner Altar submitted this memorial. The Emperor, the One of Precious Response, Primordial Sage, Martial and Civilly Wise, replied:

The Western Tibetans have repaid kindness with ingratitude, yet the Commander-in-Chief has devised a strategic plan; Heaven aids the righteous, and the leader of the wicked has been destroyed. That the soldiers and their ranks may now be released from captivity should also be a source of consolation.

I am glad to know this. A Memorial by the Monk Huichao on the Occasion of Praying for Rain at the Jade Maiden Pool (Yunütan). One memorial on praying for rain at the Jade Maiden Pool, together with the response to the Śramaṇa Huichao.
I have respectfully received the oral edict proclaimed by Imperial Messenger Li Xiancheng on the twenty-sixth day of last month,
ordering Hui-chao to proceed to the Jade Maiden Pool in Zhuzi County to maintain the incense offerings and pray for rain.
Hui-chao, while serving in the imperial palace, cultivated his practice with meticulous diligence.
He falsely proclaimed himself the mouthpiece of the Imperial Will;
thus, the spiritual responses of the mountains and rivers were never obscured when he offered prayers.
When the ritual altar was first established, the sound of the mountain stream suddenly roared;
when the śarīra relics were cast in, rain fell in threads like silk.
In a single night, the grasses and trees flourished with blossoms.
After two nights, the streams and plains were flooded with runoff;
the marshes that had been parched became deep with water.
Thus, blessings were bestowed upon both humans and spirits.
I humbly submit that Your Majesty’s sagely virtue moves Heaven, and thus the celestial bounty has first descended.
How could such gracious kindness fail to reach even the most minute creatures? It is through the resonance of your sincere devotion that this has come to pass.
I am overwhelmed with the utmost joy and exultation.
I hereby respectfully submit this memorial to offer my congratulations, taking advantage of the arrival of the imperial envoy Li Xiancheng to present it for Your Majesty’s perusal.
The śramaṇa Huichao, with the deepest humility and trepidation, speaks thus.
On the fifth day of the second month in the ninth year of the Dali era, the śramaṇa Huichao of the Inner Palace Sanctuary submitted this memorial. The Emperor Baoying Yuansheng Wencu replied:
"I am diligent in my concern for the common people."
Longing for a deep, timely rain,
he dispatched messengers throughout his village and countryside to offer prayers at all the sacred shrines.
Yet, harmonious moisture has repeatedly descended;
barely ten days have passed since the Master,
having long labored with devotion and purity, [performed the rites].
Diligently purifying the site of practice for years to come—
this brings me increased joy and celebration.
Respectfully acknowledged.
A Memorial of Congratulations for the Prayer for Rain by the Monk Tánzhēng, identical in text to the previous one. The Śramaṇas Tánzhēng and others state:
We have humbly received the imperial decree proclaimed on the twenty-ninth day of the preceding month by the Imperial Messenger Lǐ Xiàochéng.
He commanded Tan-zhen and others to recite mantras at the base of the Jade Maiden Pond (Yunütan) in front of the temple to assist in the prayers for rain.
He further submitted: "We humbly observe that there has been no accumulated snow in winter and the spring has likewise suffered from drought."
Concerned for the welfare of the common people,
he offered sincere prayers from afar;
the imperial envoys first lit the incense and candles.
The heavens were free of even a speck of dust;
once the imperial decree was proclaimed,
a mysterious spiritual transformation occurred.
The mountain winds rustle and swirl;
they are like rolling thunder.
The waters of the deep pool are still and profound.
Or it may be divided like the leaping of dragons,
so that a great downpour of abundant moisture is spread everywhere across the rivers and plains.
From this, the essence of the water-god (Ren) arose from the veins;
grasses and trees thereby sprouted their buds and split open.
The common people rejoiced and looked up to him with devotion.
Their daily practices are difficult to describe.
During the era when Tan Zhen and others were studying the Way,
they dwelt in seclusion within mountain ravines.
Fortunate to have been moistened by the Imperial Grace,
my joy and exultation increase beyond measure.
I am unable to express the height of my celebration.
I respectfully submit this memorial to report that I have presented my congratulations through the Imperial Messenger Li Xiancheng.
We, the śramaṇas Tanzheng and others, speak with utmost reverence and trepidation.

On the third day of the second month of the ninth year of the Dali era, the monk Tanzheng of Xianyousi Temple in Zhuzi County presents this memorial. The Imperial Response by Emperor Baoying Yuansheng Wenwu is the same as before. A Memorial from the Daoist Monk Daorun of Lingyingtai Congratulating on the Pacification of Henan. A Single Memorial from the Daoist Monk Daorun of Lingyingtai Congratulating on the Pacification of Henan. The Śramaṇas Daorun and others, who attend to the recitation at the Inspected Avalokiteśvara Sanctuary of Lingyingtai, say: [Text continues...]
I have humbly received the report that the various generals of Henan have captured Bianzhou,
decisively defeated Tian Huang, and taken Lingyao alive.
The faction led by Xiao Jing has disintegrated like falling snow within ten days.
The venom of bees and scorpions has melted away like ice;
Heaven, Earth, humans, and the spirits all rejoice and celebrate.
We humbly pray that Your Majesty, the Emperor, the Treasure-Response, Primordial Sage, Martial and Civil, may long reign.
Relying upon the orthodox teachings of the Dharma King,
he practiced the great compassion of Avalokiteśvara to nurture all living beings with paternal kindness.
Fearing that even a single thing might be out of place,
that mad youth will stubbornly resist and oppose Heaven; this is truly not a punishment from Heaven,
but a calamity he has brought upon himself.
Now the rivers are clear and the seas are calm;
the sun moistens all and the mountains are bright.
Yet we hear that the Celestial Master still exerts his remaining vigor, and the execution of the rebel successor is surely not far off.
At this time, how great is the monk’s joy!
By looking up to and receiving the Imperial Grace,
even the rivers and seas are not deep enough to contain it.
I am filled with the utmost joy and cannot contain my delight.
I respectfully submit this memorial to convey my congratulations, sent along with the imperial envoy Li Xiancheng.
I, the śramaṇa Daorun, most sincerely offer my congratulations and rejoice. Respectfully stated.

On the twenty-ninth day of the seventh month in the eleventh year of the Dali era, the śramaṇa Daorun, acting as inspector of the ritual site at Lingying Terrace, submitted this memorial. The Supervising Commissioner Xiancheng presented this memorial on the feathers of frightened pigeons. One Memorial on the Feathers of Frightened Pigeons Submitted by the Subject Xiancheng: Your Servant Xiancheng says:
With utmost reverence and trepidation, we acknowledge our own death-like guilt.
We humbly reflect that Your Majesty governs the world through filial piety;
it is for this reason that the mountains and rivers bestow auspicious omens.
From humans down to insects,
even those with scales and feathers manifest auspicious omens;
this is now fully recorded in the Buddhist scriptures.
Like a frightened pigeon fleeing from a hawk,
[the disciple] reached the shadow of Śāriputra, yet his trembling did not cease;
upon reaching the shadow of the Tathāgata, his fear was entirely dispelled.
The man and his bones have both long since decayed;
only the pigeon’s remaining feathers still survive today.
Its substance is light.
Its color was deep blue;
it would not burn when placed in fire,
and it would fly away whenever it encountered wind.
Your servant Xian has long served at Your Majesty’s court.
Having personally witnessed and tested that burning hair leaves no residue,
I know that the Buddha-dharma has not yet declined.
In transmitting [the legacy] from the Zhou to the Tang,
it manifests that the imperial kalpa extends even further;
such is the devotion of this dog-like servant.
I present this as an offering of wild celery;
my filial sentiments are like those of a crow or a bird,
and I feel ashamed when compared to the offerings of others.
"Though the matter is of the smallest importance, I dare not fail to present it.
Your servant Li Xiancheng, most truly prostrate and fearful, commits this to death—committing this to death!—respectfully submits these words.

On the first day of the first month of the twelfth year of Dali, submitted by Your Servant Li Xiancheng, a former attendant, Chao-san-dafu, acting as Inner Attendant-in-Waiting, Director of the Palace of the Inner Audience, concurrently holding the rank of Zhengyuan, Grand Marshal with the Rank of Shangzhu-guo, and recipient of the Fish Bag. The Emperor, the Most Precious, the Primordial Sage, Martial and Civilly Wise, replied:
As a close minister, you have protected and upheld the Śākya teachings;
through long-standing diligence,
your sincere contributions have become quite manifest.
The pigeon feathers you have presented are truly delightful.
This has been submitted for Your Majesty’s knowledge. *Dapianzheng Guangzhi Sanzang Biaozhiji*, Volume Five.

Collected Imperial Edicts and Memorials for the Venerable Upādhyāya of the Tripitaka, Great Master of Correct and Extensive Wisdom, Posthumously Honored as Minister of Works during the Reign of Emperor Daizong.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Yuanzhao of Ximing Monastery in Chang’an, the Capital. Volume Six.
A total of thirty-three pieces, consisting of twenty-two original compositions and eleven responses to imperial edicts.

One memorial submitted by the Surveillance Commissioner Li Xiancheng regarding the presentation of a *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* inscribed in golden characters, along with one response to the memorial celebrating the subjugation of Li Lingyao. [Endorsed by] the Monk.

One Memorial Requesting Ordination for Monks by Yuan Jiao; One Memorial of Thanks for Received Gifts by the Monk Changqing; One Song on Ascending the Blade Ladder with Preface by the Śramaṇa Chonghui; One Eulogy on Ascending the Blade Ladder with Preface by the Śramaṇa Chonghui;

One Memorial of Thanks for the Bestowal of Purple Robes with Response to the Imperial Decree by the Śramaṇa Chonghui; One Memorial Submitted upon the Completion of the Restoration of Temples, Pagodas, and Images in the Capital with Response;
One Memorial Submitted Regarding the Number of Meritorious Works Performed Inside and Outside the Mañjuśrī Pavilion of Xingshan Temple with Response; and One Response to the Bestowal of Raw Silk.

Forty rolls of variegated silk and yellowish-white paper; one memorial of thanks; a decree responding to Emperor Suzong’s gracious command; one imperial edict composed for the recitation of mantras by the Tripiṭaka disciple Huìzǒu and others at the Inner Daocháng;
and an imperial decree ordering the Tripiṭaka disciple Monk Huìxiǎo to act on my behalf.
I have heard this.
A son who obtains one good thing must present it to his father;
a minister who obtains one good thing must present it to his sovereign.
Such is the case for those who have inscribed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in golden letters.
The Vulture Peak bestowed its writings, transmitting the truth upon palm leaves;
the Dragon Palace transcribed its wonders, taking the lotus as a metaphor.
Thus, these scrolls are of rare and marvelous quality.
The characters were written in golden script;
their forms resembled hanging dewdrops,
and their radiance moved like a multitude of stars.
Opening the scroll to receive and uphold [the teachings] is like the hundred flowers blooming upon trees in spring;
unfolding the text and expounding it is like flocks of wild geese rising from the vast blue sea.
It purifies and washes away the five turbidities.
Adorned with the six sense organs,
it is respectfully presented on the first day of the year while kneeling,
to manifest auspiciousness.
I humbly pray that Your Majesty may share in the longevity of the Tathāgata and prolong this period of prosperity.
I am overwhelmed by the utmost sincerity of my devotion, like that of a dog or a horse.
Respectfully presented for the Emperor’s perusal.
Your servant, Li Xiancheng, with utmost sincerity, prostrates himself thrice in humble fear and speaks.

On the first day of the first month of the thirteenth year of Dali, Li Xiancheng—Original Attendant, Chao-san-dafu, acting as Inner Eunuch of the Palace Service, recipient of the crimson fish pouch, and Shang-zhuguo—submits this memorial. The Emperor Daoying Yuansheng Wenwu replied: [The Emperor’s reply follows here.]
As you, a high-ranking official, have supervised the meritorious project,
you were able to procure this wondrous scripture for the celebration of a new beginning;
upon opening the scroll, it shines with brilliant clarity.
This is truly most praiseworthy.
I submit this for Your Majesty’s perusal.
A Memorial on the Celebration of the Pacification of Li Lingyao. One Memorial on the Celebration of the Pacification of Li Lingyao. Your Servant Xian states:
I have humbly heard that the Military Governors of Huai and Bo, Mian and others,
reverently receive Your Majesty’s sagacious counsel.
Heaven’s punishment followed his course;
the brilliant stars captured him as a prisoner;
Tianhuang met with defeat and ruin.
Sweep away the dust and smoke to the south of the river;
reclaim the prefectures and counties of Daliang;
and rescue the common people from their suffering in a world mired in mud and fire.
The Emperor proclaimed his compassionate mercy;
the myriad nations rejoiced together,
and the millions of people offered their congratulations.
To manifest the spiritual bounty of the ancestral temples and to illuminate the majestic divinity of the Sage Ruler;
as for this servant’s meager abilities—
Fortunate to have encountered this sagely age,
I hear of this great celebration;
my joy and exultation are beyond measure.
I respectfully submit this memorial to convey my congratulations through the Imperial Messenger Li Xiancheng for Your Majesty’s knowledge.
I, the subject Qian, speak with sincerity, truthfulness, and joy.

On the twenty-ninth day of the tenth month of the eleventh year of Dali, this memorial was presented by the former Officer of the Left Commandery Guard and Palace Attendant of the Hanlin Academy, the subject Zhao Qian. [Attached is] one memorial from the Śramaṇa Yuanjiao requesting the ordination of monks; the Śramaṇa Yuanjiao respectfully submits his greetings.
I humbly pray that Your Majesty’s person may enjoy ten thousand blessings.
Yuanjiao was born in Fuzhou;
I am but a lowly individual from a remote region.
May there be many blessings throughout the years.
Having attended the imperial carriage since the return from Lingwu to the capital.
Having encountered the Buddhist activities during the Chengming era,
he received the bequeathed instructions of his former master;
for the sake of the state, he forgot his own person.
I have not achieved even a hair’s breadth of merit.
Having already reached the age when one follows one's own heart's desires,
my body is entangled in chronic illness.
Having no one to attend to my needs,
I look up with longing to you, O Sage,
and pray that you will graciously grant me your compassionate pity.
There was my nephew Xiaochang,
who early on received the imperial grace and was erroneously ranked among the high offices.
Truly, he lacked the labor of serving his country;
his will was set upon the practice of leaving the household life.
Emperor Yuanjiao recognized the reality of his vocation.
He did not avoid his relatives when giving alms;
although he lived as a householder,
he was always diligent in recitation and study.
I humbly reflect that Your Sacred Grace extends even to me;
I specially beg for Your exceptional favor,
hoping to exhaust my remaining strength in service.
I, Yongxi, respond from the heights.
With the utmost sincerity and trepidation,
I respectfully take this occasion of Your Majesty’s birthday.
I respectfully submit this petition through the imperial envoy Wei Xinglin for Your Majesty’s consideration.
Should Your Heavenly Grace grant permission, I pray that it be transmitted to the relevant authorities.
I have prepared the detailed specifications as follows.
The śramaṇa Yuánjiǎo, with utmost reverence and trepidation, respectfully addresses these words.

On the ninth day of the tenth month of the thirteenth year of the Dàlì era, the śramaṇa Yuánjiǎo—former recitation monk at the Daochǎng of Chángshēng Diàn and current abbot of Bǎoshòu Sī—presents this memorial. [Also included: A memorial by the śramaṇa Chángqīng and others, thanking for the bestowal of goods; and a memorial by the śramaṇa Chángqīng and others, thanking for the funeral gifts bestowed upon their deceased teacher Huìjiān. The śramaṇas Chángqīng and others state:
I have reverently received the imperial messenger Meiting Guai’s proclamation of Your Majesty’s consolation.
You have bestowed twenty bolts of silk upon the deceased monk Huijian;
kneeling to receive them, I am filled with shame and awe.
A mixture of grief and fear overwhelmed them.
The śramaṇas Changqing and others were filled with utmost awe and trepidation.
Changqing and the others had all received their training under Huijian.
Many years have passed,
yet his practice of the Way has not been refined through austerity;
he merely extends the light of his teacher.
I prostrate in humble gratitude for Your Majesty’s compassionate benevolence;
you have bestowed upon me extraordinary honors and graciously deigned to look down upon this lowly subject.
We, the humble monks, are overcome with grief and gratitude.
We respectfully submit this memorial to express our thanks for your imperial notification.
The śramaṇas Changqing and others, in utmost humility and trepidation, speak thus.

On the twelfth day of the sixth month in the seventh year of the Dali era, the disciples Changqing and others of the late recitation monk Huijian at the Inner Daochang submitted three documents: a memorial, the *Song on Ascending the Blade Ladder* by the śramaṇa Chonghui, and the preface and eulogy for the *Song on Ascending the Blade Ladder*, along with a letter of thanks. [Dated] the twenty-eighth day of the tenth month in the year of Wushen, the third year of the Dali era of the Great Tang.
By imperial decree, a ritual arena was established at Zhangjing Monastery.
At that time, there was a śramaṇa from Jiangdong named Chonghui,
who ascended a ladder of blades.
Ascending the sword-tree,
wading through oil and charcoal cauldrons,
and sitting upon beds of awls and blades.
On this day, hundreds of officials galloped like stars across the sky and ten thousand people gathered like clouds.
There was none whose soul was not startled and who did not sigh at such an unprecedented event. King Zhao bowed his head to the ground and, with feet raised high, sang this song:
A hundred-foot sword-ladder soars into the void, A thousand peaks rise up, reaching the celestial clouds.
In the frost-bright furnace of the Bird Path hermitage, The Dragon Spring’s golden rings give birth to rainbows.
Swords become trees and blades become mountains; Arhats fly their staffs as they roam therein.
Step by step he ascends, waving his hand as he clings to the hair; The seven stars shimmer with brilliant, speckled light—white as snow and blue as ice.
Turtles’ shells and fish scales in hundreds of layers;
The four assemblies behold them, trembling with awe. Upon the summit of ten-thousand-fathom peaks, one monk is seen.
The bronze of the guest is inscribed with patterns like the color of a blue serpent; its brilliant, towering, and imposing peaks are cold and majestic.
Unwounded and unimpaired, it is difficult to fathom; this is truly the power of great compassion and liberation.
Since ancient times, martial officers have prized the art of the sword; whether brandishing it or twirling it, they never fail in their skill.
Beholding him, my gallbladder seizes with fear and my body trembles; who says that one can shift the white sun by brandishing a halberd?
Li Guang’s ancient renown for a hundred battles—how does it compare to the spiritual powers seen this day?
Clad in purple robes, he flies into the void; appearing and disappearing at will amidst the flashing of white blades.
The luster of the emerald is dark and deep; its refined radiance can benefit the śramaṇa.

*Eulogy on Songhui’s Ascending the Blade Ladder*, with Preface: From the time Emperor Ming of the Han was moved by his dream and Kāśyapa Mātaṅga and Dharmaratna tore open the net of falsehoods at Luoyang, until the Qin ruler harbored doubts and Kumārajīva revealed the precious mirror within the jar.
Fu Yi offered words of reproach and authored a "Treatise on Rectification";
Daolin and Daohui promoted heterodoxy and manifested divine efficacy at Zhangjing Temple.
As for the matter of the statue, Xuan Song erected a wooden image one hundred feet tall.
Above, there are two tiers,
with jeweled blades interlacing and golden bells surrounding them on all four sides.
Eight cauldrons of blazing furnaces surround the pool,
which is adorned with lotuses;
sharp seats and poisonous blades are arrayed together within the balustrades.
On this day, the heavens were crystalline and increasingly bright;
wind and dust did not arise;
and the hoarfrost gathered and dispersed.
The sunlight was warm and the atmosphere was bustling.
At that time, an imperial decree granted him Dharma robes,
with an official personally supervising the presentation.
National Preceptors and Ministers,
the heroic ranks of civil and military officials,
and the harmonious counselors of neighboring states.
Dharma companions, both dragon-like patriarchs and elephant-like disciples,
as well as those in yellow caps and red banners, all gathered together for the Dharma assembly;
commoners and officials filled the streets.
They stood on tiptoe, looking back and forth;
the Buddha’s voice thundered forth, heard throughout the ten directions,
while the smoke from the many jewel censers rose like clouds and canopies.
Thereupon, he crushed the sword-trees with his hands and shattered the forest of blades with his feet,
amidst fierce flames and billowing smoke.
As they came and went therein,
they spread out their sitting mats upon the ponds;
it was as if lotuses were emerging and blossoming.
Though the tips of many poisons were gathered like blades and he was pursued everywhere for his food,
he did not fall from the monastic deportment.
He rinsed his mouth and scattered [the water] about;
the great assembly all marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
I personally witnessed this magnificent event.
Overjoyed beyond measure,
we are all bathed in the compassionate clouds and rely upon being moistened by your sublime grace.
Holding aloft the torch, he shatters the darkness of the mountains,
clears away the turbid currents,
and returns to the ocean of Dharma.
The Verse says: How great is the Perfectly Awakened One! His supernormal powers are inconceivable. In a dream, Emperor Ming was moved;
Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna descended with radiance. The multitudes of heterodoxies abandoned their attachments. I bow my head in refuge.
The Qin Palace Mirror Treasure: The Vase Manifests and Subdues Doubt.
Fu Yi’s Words of Censure and Ridicule are Refuted and Crushed. By the Śramaṇa Chonghui. Stopping Slander and Dispelling Error;
Water, Fire, Blades, and Poison. A Verification of Rare Marvels.
How excellent! A magnificent event for this single lifetime, which shall not change for a thousand years to come.
A Memorial of Thanks for the Bestowal of a Purple Robe and a Memorial of Congratulations, by the Śramaṇa Chonghui. The Śramaṇa Chonghui states:
Yesterday, I received the imperial decree issued by the Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Bodyguard,
ordering me to ascend the sword-tree and cross the fire-pit at Zhangjing Temple.
Furthermore, I have humbly received the decree delivered by the Palace Messenger Gong Tingyu, bestowing upon me one set of purple monastic robes.
Having heard this,
Chonghui’s aspiration was not in vain;
the compassion of Avalokiteśvara was swift.
When one contemplates this with resolve, the response follows;
the power of the Benevolent One is so mighty that even entering fire does not burn him, ensuring that his efficacy is certain.
Stepping upon the blade, it did not cut; this was subsequently reported as a manifest sign of divine response.
I did not expect that the Great Sage would bestow his majesty and that heavenly grace would so graciously descend upon me.
Thus, one is led to contemplate the body as the Dharma-realm;
though encountering blazing flames, one remains unharmed, and with every step taken,
one reaches the site of enlightenment.
Though encountering frost and blades, they are not discouraged;
truly, it is hoped that the miasma of calamity will forever cease and the ocean of karma will remain eternally clear.
Moreover, that both monastics and laypeople rejoice together and that beings of the human and celestial realms all behold this is surely moved by Your Majesty’s utmost sincerity.
How could this be the achievement of a single humble monk’s resolve?
Having been undeservedly bathed in Your Majesty’s extraordinary favor,
I am filled with boundless joy and gratitude.
I respectfully submit this memorial to express my gratitude for Your Majesty’s knowledge of it.
The Sramana Chonghui, with utmost humility and trepidation, speaks thus.

On the twenty-ninth day of the tenth month in the third year of the Dali era, the Sramana Chonghui of Anguo Temple presents this memorial to the Emperor, the One Who Is Precious and Responding, the Primordial Sage, Martial and Civilly Wise. The Emperor replies: [The Emperor’s reply follows here.]

The Master was diligent in his pure conduct and had early attained harmony with the True Vehicle; his sincerity moved the divine, and he was protected by the Buddha's mindfulness. He cast his body upon blazing flames and placed his feet upon the tips of sharp blades, walking with composure as if upon a couch or mat. When he toured the capital and the fourfold assembly took refuge in him, they offered him gifts, yet he declined them, expressing his gratitude for their tireless efforts.

A Memorial Submitted upon the Completion of the Imperial Decree to Cleanse the Temples, Pagodas, and Images of the Capital; together with a Reply to the Śramaṇa Huiguo. One Memorial Submitted upon the Completion of the Imperial Decree to Cleanse the Temples, Pagodas, and Images of the Capital, along with a Reply to the Śramaṇa Huiguo.
I humbly acknowledge the imperial edict proclaimed by the Central Envoy Li Xiancheng on the nineteenth day of the twelfth month last year, commanding that I,
a humble monk, shall oversee the affairs of the various monasteries throughout the capital.
He swept and cleaned the palace halls,
wiped and polished the sacred images,
and exhorted the assembly of monks and nuns.
Incense was burned and recitations were performed;
for the sake of the nation, vows were made,
and blessings were reverently sought.
I respectfully record that the work commenced on the twentieth day of the twelfth month past at the Buddha’s Tooth Relic site in Zhuangyan Temple and concluded on the eighth day of this month.

This includes all temples with halls, pagodas, Buddha tooth relics, scriptural treasuries, sacred sites, and śarīra remains, totaling one hundred and twelve temples across nine hundred and fifty-seven locations, including Xingshan Temple and others.
He reverently proclaimed the sagely sincerity and brought forth the teachings of the Buddha-image,
sweeping away the dust of kalpas upon the stone.
Celestial robes of six *zhu* were descended to cleanse the dust from the golden body;
a thousand petals shone upon the lotus seat.
The ancient countenances were reflected once more,
the old books were restored to their former brilliance,
and incense was burned within the hall.
Sprinkling water within the courtyard,
he made a vow while abiding in purity;
if there were a spiritual response and a resonance with his sincerity.
Now the four seas have their waves stilled,
and the three heavens have rolled back the mists;
the dust of foreign invaders does not rise.
The rising sun breaks the gloom.
This humble monk further reverently consults such scriptures as the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra*, which state:
"If one were to sweep the ground of a single Jambudvīpa..."
It is not equal to sweeping even a single palm’s breadth of a Buddha stupa;
[the latter] ensures one will constantly become a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
These [observations] all stem from the subtle and profound deliberations of the Sage below the steps.
With profound faith, he expanded and purified the Pure Land,
broadening the gateway of emptiness;
he provided great protection for the followers of Śākya, extending his influence across ten thousand nations.
If blessings gather like clouds,
they will arrive like echoes;
thus, calamities and misfortunes shall not arise.
The ominous vapors have naturally vanished,
harmonizing with Your Majesty’s sagely intentions so swiftly; this is due to the humble monk’s efforts.
The Master and his disciples were specially favored by the Imperial Guard;
they were granted horses from the imperial stables and received the honor of being welcomed into the Inner Palace.
This glorious mandate descended from Heaven.
Filled with trepidation and at a loss for what to do,
I have been unable to contribute even a drop or a speck of merit.
How could I possibly bear such a torrential grace?
With the utmost sincerity and devotion,
I respectfully submit this memorial along with the Imperial Messenger Yuan Yingjin for Your Majesty’s perusal.
In profound awe and trepidation, I humbly conclude these words.

On the eighth day of the first month in the twelfth year of the Dali era, Śramaṇa Huiguo, serving as inspector of two *maṇḍala* sites and concurrently presiding over the affairs of the monastery at Daxingshan Temple, presented this memorial. [The Emperor] bestowed the following imperial decree upon the Ācārya for his wondrous conduct and steadfast perseverance: [To] the Illustrious, Holy, Martial, and Cultured Emperor of the Baoying Reign. [Imperial Decree: "Your practice is wondrous and your resolve is firm."
I have heard that you are renowned for your cultivation of purity;
therefore, I command you to travel throughout the pure realms to extensively cultivate supreme causes.
The golden spire is once again serene;
the jade-like radiance manifests its illumination.
Wherever one’s devotion reaches, [the response follows].
This is truly praiseworthy.
Your memorial has been brought to our knowledge.

Attached is a memorial titled "A Table of the Meritorious Deeds Performed Inside and Outside the Mañjuśrī Pavilion of Xingshan Monastery," one scroll, together with the response from within the Mañjuśrī State-Protection Pavilion of Daxingshan Monastery.
By Imperial Decree, one set of nine figures of the Six-Syllable Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī was executed in plain line-drawing;
furthermore, one hundred and four figures of the sacred assembly of Mañjuśrī’s retinue were painted on the interior and exterior walls of the pavilion.
Now both have been accomplished.
The śramaṇa Huisheng reports:
I humbly reflect upon Your Majesty, the Emperor, the Treasure-Response, Primordial Sage, Martial and Civil Sovereign.
He extensively propagated the deeds of Mañjuśrī and practiced the vows of Samantabhadra for the benefit of all living beings.
Planting these supreme causes,
it manifests the true form of the fruits of virtue and reveals the real nature of the form-body.
Now that the seven calamities have been dispelled and all blessings are manifest,
had it not been for Your Majesty’s sacred compassion, [this would not have been possible].
By what means can one behold the vermilion doors, where the morning candles shine like the sun-palace,
and the jade-hair radiance glows like the moon-palace at night?
Those who rejoice in this merit owe it to the power of the Emperor.
Those who take refuge have resolved their minds upon Bodhi,
so that sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges may universally receive the Buddha’s bounty;
yet among them, the monastics of the dark gate are especially bathed in the imperial grace.
How could merely turning the beads, reciting,
and upholding [the mantra] suffice to repay [one's debts]?
I only hope to rely upon the spiritual power of Mañjuśrī.
To repay the great grace bestowed upon me,
I have respectfully prepared this painted scroll of the Great Sage’s Field of Merit on this auspicious occasion of his birth.
Respectfully submitted by the Imperial Messenger Li Xiancheng, presenting this memorial for the Emperor’s perusal.
The Śramaṇa Huisheng, with utmost humility and trepidation, respectfully states:

On the eighth day of the tenth month of the twelfth year of the Dali era, the Śramaṇa Huisheng, who serves as the Inspector of the Two Monasteries and Overseer of Monastic Affairs, submits this memorial to the Most Gracious, Most Holy, Martial, and Civil Emperor. The Emperor’s Edict: “The Master has long been diligent in his Buddhist practice.”
His observance of the precepts was rigorous and strict;
he had long dwelt in the place of practice (bodhimaṇḍa),
establishing his lineage through earnest virtue.
Their labors manifest through the passing of years and months;
blessings accumulate within the family and the state;
these are immeasurable and supreme causes.
This is the expression of consolation and praise.

A memorial of thanks for the imperial gift of forty bolts of cotton, silk, and fine cloth; a memorial of thanks for the imperial gift of forty bolts of brocade, silk, and fine cloth; and a reply to the śramaṇa Huisheng. One copy each.
I have humbly received the imperial decree proclaimed by the Palace Messenger Li Xiancheng,
graciously bestowing upon me forty rolls of brocade, silk, and fine cloth. As I receive them while kneeling in prostration,
I am filled with shame and gratitude.
I am overwhelmed with both joy and trepidation.
I humbly beseech Your Majesty,
the Emperor, the Treasure-Response, Primordial Sage, Martial and Civil Ruler.

The bodies of emanation of all Buddhas and the secret conduct of Samantabhadra manifest as vast transformations; thus, though the Honored Among Men has humbled himself, these sublime blessings have been bestowed specifically upon this humble monk.
Now, regarding the Dharma of Samantabhadra:
This is originally the scripture transmitted by my former teacher and is further the Way entrusted to Your Majesty.
This humble monk is deeply moved from afar by the bequeathed instructions of my former teacher.
Looking upward, I am filled with shame before the profound grace of the Holy Sovereign;
emulating the ancients in the practice of offering humble greens,
I present this mere drop so that it may reach Your Majesty’s heart.
Unexpectedly, the imperial grace bestowed upon me was exceedingly great;
I have therefore taken what was granted and offered it at the shadow-image stupa of my late master,
performing recitations for the sake of the nation.
In these various assemblies and places of practice,
they made their vows with sincere earnestness,
hoping to rely upon the power of the Buddha.
I pray that the Imperial House may enjoy eternal stability.
Overwhelmed by the utmost sense of gratitude and indebtedness,
I have respectfully attached this memorial to the imperial envoy Li Xiancheng to express my thanks and report this to Your Majesty.
Respectfully addressed by the Śramaṇa Huisheng, who is truly joyful and congratulatory.

On the sixth day of the sixth month in the thirteenth year of the Dali era, the Śramaṇa Huisheng—Director of Affairs and Inspector of the Two Doctrinal Halls at Daxingshan Monastery—presents this memorial to the Emperor, the One of Precious Response, the Primordial Sage, the Martial and Civilly Wise. An imperial edict concerning the secret treasury of all Buddhas.
Our former master received and upheld it,
transmitting it to humans and devas;
it is truly a vital essential of the Dharma.
I have briefly submitted this token of encouragement and reward to assist in your spiritual cultivation.
Please be informed of my gratitude.

An Imperial Decree by Emperor Suzong Ordering the Tripiṭaka Master’s Disciple Huìzǒu to Enter the Inner Sanctuary for Recitation One Poem: An Imperial Decree by Emperor Suzong Ordering the Tripiṭaka Master’s Disciple Huìzǒu to Enter the Inner Sanctuary for Recitation In accordance with the Imperial Edict, the attendants of the Yintai Gate were summoned to call the four disciples of the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra—Huìzǒu, Juna, Huìxiǎo, and Huìyuè—to enter the palace.
The Flying Dragon Horse was taken to provide for the Tripitaka Master’s adornment of the ritual arena and his recitations.

On the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month of the second year of Zhidu, the Court Official Yan Ru Zhang proclaimed an imperial edict ordering the Tripitaka Master’s disciple, the monk Huixiao, to perform recitations for the state. An imperial decree was issued appointing the Tripitaka Master’s disciple, the monk Huixiao, to perform recitations for the state. One copy of this decree was presented to the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra’s disciple, the monk Huixiao, etc., with the Imperial Command stating: "To the disciples of the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra, including the monk Huixiao..."
While you were among the rebels,
you cultivated mindfulness with sincere devotion and secretly practiced meritorious deeds for my sake;
now that the empire has been reclaimed, [I recognize your merit].
All of this is a response to the Buddha’s power.
From this day forward,
you must redouble your diligent efforts.
Recite [the scriptures] for me.
Do not think that because you have attained liberation you need no longer apply yourself with diligence.

On the eighteenth day of the first month of the third year of Zhìdé, General Duán Qiáofú proclaimed the imperial decree of Emperor Dàizōng ordering Xìmíng Monastery to provide gruel and meals, as well as horses and carriages for travel. This is the single decree issued by Emperor Dàizōng ordering Xìmíng Monastery to provide gruel and meals, as well as horses and carriages for travel. It is issued by imperial command to the monk Huìxiǎo of Xìmíng Monastery.
On my behalf, cultivate merit;
remain at the monastery as usual,
and for the two daily meals of gruel and rice, as well as for the mounts used for coming and going, provide them accordingly.
Ensure that all provisions are supplied without deficiency.

On the twenty-fifth day of the eighth month of the sixth year of the Dali era, the High Official Ma Fengcheng proclaimed the imperial decree for departing Mount Wutai to cultivate merit. A memorial of thanks for the imperial favor regarding the departure for Mount Wutai to cultivate merit; one memorial of thanks for the imperial favor, together with the response to the śramaṇa Huixiao.
On the tenth day of this month, I received your instructions in person,
ordering me to go to Mount Wutai to inspect the color, features, and mudras of the sacred images at the Great Holy Jingetemple.
I shall cease my work in the ninth month.
He then proceeded to the imperial court and was ordered to perform meritorious rites for the Emperor’s birthday.
Hui-xiao had, since twenty years prior, left his home out of a longing for the Way.
For over thirty years, he served and followed the countenance of the Great and Vast Wisdom Tripitaka Master,
never departing from his side; the mantras of the five classes were personally transmitted to him through direct instruction.
Having been granted an audience with Your Majesty’s countenance,
I have constantly cultivated merit in the Hanyi, Yanying, Changsheng, and other halls;
my only regret is that I am unable to do so with utmost sincerity.
While the remaining rebels have not yet been pacified,
Your Majesty’s sacred compassion has looked down upon us with particular kindness.
You have further commanded a distant envoy to bestow thirty rolls of fine silk, along with provisions for the postal relay horses and the loan of mounts from the mountain gate.
How fortunate this humble monk is that the imperial grace has been repeatedly bestowed upon him!
I am truly joyful and delighted, and my sense of gratitude is beyond measure.
I shall set out this very day.
One may truly be said to ride upon a flying steed,
gazing at the Golden Pavilion as if it were not far away;
thus one departs in spring and returns in autumn.
To behold the Purple Shaking (the Emperor) would be no distance away;
I am overwhelmed by the utmost longing for his grace and by trepidation.
